subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which field in a block header links the block to its predecessor?
option_1: The hash of the previous block's header
option_2: The Merkle root of the previous block's transactions
option_3: The nonce used to mine the previous block
option_4: The timestamp of the genesis block
answer_text: The hash of the previous block's header
explanation: Each header stores the hash of the previous header, which turns the chain into a hash-pointer list: changing an old block changes its hash and breaks the next link. The Merkle root is also in the header, but it commits to this block's own transactions, not to the previous block.
concept: Blocks are chained by storing the previous header's hash.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which hash-function property makes it computationally infeasible to find any two distinct inputs with the same digest?
option_1: Preimage resistance (one-wayness)
option_2: The avalanche effect
option_3: Collision resistance
option_4: Second-preimage resistance
answer_text: Collision resistance
explanation: Collision resistance lets the attacker choose both inputs freely and still demands that no colliding pair can be found. Second-preimage resistance is the tempting answer, but there the first input is fixed in advance, which is a harder task for the attacker and therefore a weaker requirement.
concept: Collision: any pair x≠x′ with h(x)=h(x′); second preimage: x is given.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does the Merkle root in a Bitcoin block header commit to?
option_1: Only the coinbase transaction, which pays the block reward to the miner
option_2: The full set of unspent transaction outputs across the network
option_3: The hashes of all earlier block headers back to the genesis block
option_4: Every transaction in the block, via a tree of pairwise hashes
answer_text: Every transaction in the block, via a tree of pairwise hashes
explanation: Transaction hashes are paired and hashed level by level until one root remains, so changing any transaction changes the root and hence the header hash. Commitment to earlier headers comes from the previous-hash field, not the Merkle root; Bitcoin headers do not commit to the UTXO set at all.
concept: Merkle root = single hash committing to all transactions in the block.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In Proof of Work, when is a candidate block's header hash acceptable?
option_1: When the hash equals the hash of the previous block
option_2: When the hash, as a number, is below the target
option_3: When the hash is above the current difficulty value
option_4: When the hash, read as a number, is a prime number
answer_text: When the hash, as a number, is below the target
explanation: The puzzle is H(header) < T: a lower target admits fewer hashes and so needs more expected work. Difficulty and target move in opposite directions, so 'above the difficulty' reverses the rule.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: During a network partition a protocol stops making progress, but it never lets two honest nodes commit conflicting blocks. Which property has it preserved?
option_1: Liveness
option_2: Availability
option_3: Termination
option_4: Safety
answer_text: Safety
explanation: Safety means nothing bad happens: no conflicting commits. It can hold even while progress stalls. Liveness and its per-instance form, termination, are exactly what the stalled protocol has given up.
concept: Safety = no conflicting decisions; liveness = eventual progress.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.2

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In Hyperledger Fabric, what does MSP stand for?
option_1: Membership Service Provider
option_2: Message Sequencing Peer
option_3: Membership Signing Protocol
option_4: Managed Service Provider
answer_text: Membership Service Provider
explanation: The MSP defines which root CAs an organisation trusts, how identities are validated and which roles they hold. 'Managed Service Provider' is a common slip from IT outsourcing vocabulary and is wrong in Fabric.
concept: MSP maps certificates to organisations and roles.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A client presents a valid X.509 certificate issued by its organisation's CA. What has been established at this point?
option_1: Authorization to invoke every chaincode function on the channel
option_2: Authorization for every role named in the CA's root certificate
option_3: Authentication: who the caller is, but not yet what it may do
option_4: Confidentiality of all the caller's future transactions
answer_text: Authentication: who the caller is, but not yet what it may do
explanation: A certificate proves identity (authentication). Authorization still has to be checked separately against roles, attributes, ownership or endorsement policy. Treating a valid certificate as full access is a classic design error.
concept: Authentication = who you are; authorization = what you may do.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In Bitcoin's UTXO model, what does a transaction input reference?
option_1: A specific earlier output, identified by txid and output index
option_2: An account balance held in the global state trie of the network
option_3: The height of the block in which the coins were originally mined
option_4: The sender's address together with an incrementing account nonce
answer_text: A specific earlier output, identified by txid and output index
explanation: Bitcoin has no accounts; each input points to one unspent output (txid:index) and must satisfy its locking script. Address-plus-nonce is the account model used by Ethereum, which is why it is a tempting but wrong answer here.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.3

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which consensus mechanism relies on a trusted execution environment to attest a random waiting time?
option_1: Proof of Burn (PoB)
option_2: Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS)
option_3: Proof of Elapsed Time (PoET)
option_4: Leased Proof of Stake (LPoS)
answer_text: Proof of Elapsed Time (PoET)
explanation: In PoET each node waits a random time attested by a TEE such as Intel SGX, and the shortest wait wins; Hyperledger Sawtooth used it. Its trust therefore rests on the hardware vendor. DPoS uses elected producers and involves no special hardware.
concept: PoET = TEE-attested random wait; trust shifts to hardware.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.8

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How does Alice prove that she authorised a transaction in a way anyone can check?
option_1: She encrypts it with her own public key so only she can open it
option_2: She signs it with her private key; anyone verifies with her public key
option_3: She signs it with the recipient's public key so the recipient can verify
option_4: She attaches a MAC computed with a key shared with the recipient
answer_text: She signs it with her private key; anyone verifies with her public key
explanation: Only the private-key holder can produce the signature, and the public key lets anyone verify it. A MAC also gives integrity, but it uses a shared secret, so third parties cannot verify it and the recipient could have forged it.
concept: Digital signature: sign with private key, verify with public key.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In role-based access control, to what are permissions assigned?
option_1: To attributes evaluated by a policy engine at request time
option_2: To roles; users gain permissions by being assigned to roles
option_3: To security labels compared against clearances
option_4: Directly to individual users by the resource owner
answer_text: To roles; users gain permissions by being assigned to roles
explanation: RBAC puts roles between users and permissions, so administrators manage a small set of roles instead of per-user grants. Owner-granted rights describe DAC and labels describe MAC.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why are Bitcoin addresses described as pseudonymous rather than anonymous?
option_1: The protocol forbids reusing any address for a second payment
option_2: Exchanges are legally barred from linking addresses to identities
option_3: Addresses are encrypted on chain so that only miners can read them
option_4: Addresses aren't real names, but their public transactions can be linked
answer_text: Addresses aren't real names, but their public transactions can be linked
explanation: An address hides a legal name but the public ledger records all its flows, so clustering heuristics and exchange records can link it to a person. Nothing in the protocol encrypts addresses or forbids reuse.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.6

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An MD5 input is 1000 bits long. How many padding bits are appended before the 64-bit length field, and what is the final padded length?
option_1: 448 padding bits; 1512 bits in total
option_2: 472 padding bits; 1536 bits in total
option_3: 472 padding bits; 1472 bits in total
option_4: 24 padding bits; 1088 bits in total
answer_text: 472 padding bits; 1536 bits in total
explanation: Padding (a 1 then zeros) must bring the length to 448 mod 512: 1000 mod 512 = 488, so the next value ≡ 448 is 1472, which needs 472 bits; adding the 64-bit length gives 1536 = 3 × 512. The 1472 answer forgets the length field, and 24 bits simply rounds to the next 512-bit boundary.
concept: MD5 pad to 448 mod 512, then append 64-bit length.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A toy chain uses a 16-bit hash and accepts a block when the hash is below T = 2^10. A miner computes 16 hashes per second. What are the expected hashes per block and the expected time?
option_1: 1,024 hashes, about 64 seconds
option_2: 64 hashes, about 4 seconds
option_3: 6 hashes, under 1 second
option_4: 32 hashes, about 2 seconds
answer_text: 64 hashes, about 4 seconds
explanation: P(success) = T/2^16 = 2^10/2^16 = 1/64, so the expected number of hashes is 64 and 64/16 = 4 s. The 1,024 answer confuses the target value with the expected work.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: The last 2016 Bitcoin blocks took 12 days instead of the intended 14. What happens to the difficulty at the retarget?
option_1: It falls by about ×0.857 because the blocks came early
option_2: It doubles, to restore the two-week schedule at once
option_3: It stays the same, since changes under ×4 are ignored
option_4: It rises by about ×1.167 (the target shrinks to ×0.857)
answer_text: It rises by about ×1.167 (the target shrinks to ×0.857)
explanation: D_new = D_old × 14/12 ≈ 1.167, because blocks came too fast and the puzzle must get harder. The ×4 clamp only limits extreme adjustments; it does not suppress small ones. Applying 12/14 instead inverts the direction.
concept: D_new = D_old × (expected time / actual time), clamped to [¼, 4].
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An ordering service must tolerate f = 2 Byzantine nodes. What is the minimum number of nodes and the quorum size?
option_1: 7 nodes with a quorum of 5
option_2: 5 nodes with a quorum of 3
option_3: 7 nodes with a quorum of 4
option_4: 6 nodes with a quorum of 4
answer_text: 7 nodes with a quorum of 5
explanation: BFT needs n ≥ 3f + 1 = 7 and quorums of 2f + 1 = 5, so any two quorums overlap in at least one honest node. Five nodes with quorum 3 is the crash-fault (Raft) sizing for f = 2 and does not survive lying nodes.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An attacker controls 20% of the hash power and a merchant waits for 4 confirmations. Using the simplified catch-up model P = (q/p)^z, what is the attacker's success probability?
explanation: With q = 0.2 and p = 0.8, q/p = 1/4 and (1/4)^4 = 1/256 ≈ 0.39%. Using q alone ignores the honest chain's progress, which is why (0.2)^4 understates the risk.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.2 & ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A block contains 1,000 transactions. How many sibling hashes does a Merkle proof of membership for one transaction contain?
explanation: A balanced binary tree over 1,000 leaves has depth ⌈log2 1000⌉ = 10, and the proof carries one sibling per level. Linear answers such as 999 describe re-hashing everything, which is what the Merkle tree avoids.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Alice owns UTXOs of 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 BTC. She pays Bob 0.7 BTC with a 0.01 BTC fee, spending the 0.5 and 0.3 outputs. What change output should the transaction create?
option_1: 0.29 BTC back to Alice
option_2: No change output, since the fee absorbs the remainder
option_3: 0.10 BTC back to Alice
option_4: 0.09 BTC back to Alice
answer_text: 0.09 BTC back to Alice
explanation: Inputs total 0.8 BTC; outputs must total 0.8 − 0.01 = 0.79, so Bob gets 0.7 and change is 0.09. Leaving out the change output would hand the miner 0.1 BTC as fee, and 0.29 wrongly includes the unspent 0.2 UTXO.
concept: Fee = Σinputs − Σoutputs; change returns the rest.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.3

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Policy OutOf(2, 'Mfr.peer', 'Dist.peer', 'Hosp.peer'). A transaction endorsed only by Mfr's peer is still submitted to the orderer. What happens?
option_1: Rejected by the orderer, so it never appears in any block at all
option_2: Included in a block but flagged invalid; world state unchanged
option_3: Included in a block but flagged MVCC_READ_CONFLICT by the peers
option_4: Committed, because OutOf needs only one endorsement per organisation
answer_text: Included in a block but flagged invalid; world state unchanged
explanation: The orderer only orders and does not evaluate chaincode endorsement policies, so the transaction enters a block. Committing peers then run VSCC, find one signature where two are required, and mark it invalid while keeping it for audit. MVCC conflicts concern stale read versions, not missing signatures.
concept: Endorsement policy is checked by committing peers at validation.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Tx1 and Tx2 both read key BATCH-1001 at version (5,0) and write it. The orderer places Tx1 before Tx2 in block 6. What is the outcome?
option_1: Both invalid, because they conflict with each other in the block
option_2: Tx1 valid; Tx2 invalid (MVCC_READ_CONFLICT); both stay in block 6
option_3: Tx1 valid; the orderer removes Tx2 from block 6 before delivery
option_4: Both valid, because each carries the required valid endorsements
answer_text: Tx1 valid; Tx2 invalid (MVCC_READ_CONFLICT); both stay in block 6
explanation: Tx1 commits first and moves the key to a new version, so Tx2's read version (5,0) is stale at validation. Endorsement does not mean commit. The orderer never inspects read-write sets, so it cannot drop Tx2.
concept: MVCC: a read version must still be current at commit time.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Under Bell–LaPadula, a subject cleared for Secret tries (i) to read a Top Secret file and (ii) to write a Confidential file. What is the result?
option_1: Both are allowed because Secret dominates Confidential
option_2: The read is denied and the write is allowed
option_3: Both are denied: no read up and no write down
option_4: The read is allowed and the write is denied
answer_text: Both are denied: no read up and no write down
explanation: The simple-security property forbids reading above one's clearance, and the *-property forbids writing to a lower level so secrets cannot leak downward. Many people accept the write because Confidential is lower, but that is exactly the downward flow BLP blocks.
concept: BLP (confidentiality): no read up, no write down.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Approximately how many random hash evaluations give a 50% chance of a collision on a 64-bit digest?
option_2: About 9.2 × 10^18 (2^63, half the space)
option_3: About 1.8 × 10^19 (2^64, the full space)
option_4: About 75 (1.17 × 64 digest bits)
explanation: The birthday bound is Q ≈ 1.17√M with M = 2^64, giving about 1.17 × 2^32 ≈ 5.06 × 10^9. 2^63 or 2^64 is the cost of a preimage-style search, not of finding any colliding pair.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Ethereum uses 12-second slots and 32-slot epochs, and finality normally arrives after about two epochs. Roughly how long is that?
option_1: About 6.4 minutes
option_2: About 60 minutes
option_3: About 12.8 minutes
option_4: About 64 seconds
answer_text: About 12.8 minutes
explanation: One epoch is 32 × 12 s = 384 s = 6.4 min, and two epochs give 12.8 min. 6.4 minutes is the length of one epoch, which is only enough to justify a checkpoint, not to finalize it.
concept: Slot 12 s, epoch 6.4 min, finality ≈ 2 epochs.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A chaincode function stamps each record with time.Now() and the policy requires endorsements from two organisations. What is the most likely failure?
option_1: Nothing fails, since peers keep their clocks synchronised by NTP
option_2: Every such transaction fails at commit with MVCC_READ_CONFLICT
option_3: The orderer re-executes it and rejects it as non-deterministic code
option_4: Endorsers return different read-write sets, so endorsements don't match
answer_text: Endorsers return different read-write sets, so endorsements don't match
explanation: Each peer simulates independently, and wall-clock values differ, so the signed results do not match. The orderer never executes chaincode. The deterministic fix is to use the transaction timestamp (GetTxTimestamp) or pass the time as an argument.
concept: Chaincode must be deterministic across endorsers.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: User U is to be assigned both the Clerk role {read, create} and the Auditor role {read, export}. A static separation-of-duty constraint declares Clerk and Auditor mutually exclusive. What should the system do?
option_1: Reject the assignment: static SoD forbids holding both roles
option_2: Allow it, provided U activates only one role per session
option_3: Grant U only the intersection of both roles: {read}
option_4: Grant U the union of both roles: {read, create, export}
answer_text: Reject the assignment: static SoD forbids holding both roles
explanation: Static SoD constrains role assignment itself, so the second assignment must be refused. Activating one role per session describes dynamic SoD, which is a different and weaker constraint than the one stated.
concept: Static SoD restricts assignment; dynamic SoD restricts activation.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Five hospitals must share patient-referral records. All participants are known, the records are confidential, throughput must be high, and no hospital trusts another to run a central database. Which design fits best?
option_1: A permissioned ledger such as Fabric, with channels or PDCs
option_2: A central database operated by the largest hospital in the group
option_3: A public PoW blockchain storing the referral records in plaintext
option_4: A public PoS chain with a gas fee charged on every record write
answer_text: A permissioned ledger such as Fabric, with channels or PDCs
explanation: Known members, confidentiality and throughput point to a permissioned ledger secured by identity and governance. A central database is ruled out by the stated lack of trust, and public chains expose data and add cost without any need for open membership.
concept: Use permissioned DLT when parties are known but mutually distrustful.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain, decentralization chapter

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A pool with 30% of the hash power considers selfish mining. It loses every block race (γ = 0). Using the threshold (1 − γ)/(3 − 2γ), is the strategy profitable?
option_1: No: selfish mining only works with more than 50%
option_2: Yes: selfish mining is profitable at any pool size
option_3: No: at γ = 0 the threshold is 1/3, above the pool's 30%
option_4: Yes: any pool above 25% profits from selfish mining
answer_text: No: at γ = 0 the threshold is 1/3, above the pool's 30%
explanation: At γ = 0 the threshold is 1/3, and 30% falls below it, so withheld blocks are lost too often. The 25% figure applies only when γ = 1/2, and 'any size' only when γ = 1. Selfish mining does not need a majority, which is exactly why it matters.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A consortium has Mfr, Dist, Hosp and Reg. Every batch transfer must be approved by the manufacturer and by at least one of the distributor or hospital; the regulator must never be required. Which endorsement policy meets this exactly?
option_1: AND('Mfr.peer', OR('Dist.peer', 'Hosp.peer'))
option_2: AND('Mfr.peer', 'Dist.peer', 'Hosp.peer', 'Reg.peer')
option_3: OR('Mfr.peer', AND('Dist.peer', 'Hosp.peer'))
option_4: OutOf(2, 'Mfr.peer', 'Dist.peer', 'Hosp.peer')
answer_text: AND('Mfr.peer', OR('Dist.peer', 'Hosp.peer'))
explanation: The AND forces Mfr and the inner OR accepts either Dist or Hosp, with Reg absent. OutOf(2, …) looks close, but Dist + Hosp would satisfy it without the manufacturer. The OR variant lets Mfr approve alone.
concept: Compose AND/OR/OutOf to encode exact approval rules.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: On a four-organisation channel, pricing must be visible only to Mfr and Dist, yet the other members must be able to verify later that a price record existed and was not altered. Which design satisfies this?
option_1: Create a separate Mfr–Dist channel; its hashes appear on the main channel automatically
option_2: Restrict the query function by MSP ID while storing the price in public world state
option_3: Rely on an endorsement policy AND('Mfr.peer','Dist.peer') to hide the price
option_4: A Mfr–Dist private data collection, with only the price hash on the channel ledger
answer_text: A Mfr–Dist private data collection, with only the price hash on the channel ledger
explanation: A PDC disseminates the data only to member peers while the hash on the shared ledger lets anyone verify a later disclosure. A query check hides nothing, because every channel peer still stores the plaintext. Endorsement policies control who signs, not who sees, and channels do not cross-post hashes.
concept: PDC = private data off-ledger for a subset; hash on-ledger for all.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the genesis block?
option_1: The block containing the most transactions so far
option_2: The newest block, at the current tip of the chain
option_3: The first block, which has no predecessor
option_4: A block created after every difficulty retarget
answer_text: The first block, which has no predecessor
explanation: The genesis block is hard-coded as block 0, so its previous-hash field points to no real block. Every other block descends from it through hash links. The chain tip is the most recent block, not the first.
concept: Genesis block = block 0, the root of the chain.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What are MD5's digest size and message block size?
option_1: 160-bit digest, 512-bit blocks
option_2: 256-bit digest, 1024-bit blocks
option_3: 128-bit digest, 512-bit blocks
option_4: 128-bit digest, 1024-bit blocks
answer_text: 128-bit digest, 512-bit blocks
explanation: MD5 processes 512-bit blocks through 4 rounds of 16 steps and outputs a 128-bit digest held in four 32-bit buffers. The 160-bit digest belongs to SHA-1, which uses the same 512-bit block size.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How often does Bitcoin recompute its mining difficulty?
option_1: Every 144 blocks (about one day)
option_2: Every 210,000 blocks
option_3: Every 2016 blocks (about two weeks)
option_4: After every block
answer_text: Every 2016 blocks (about two weeks)
explanation: Bitcoin retargets every 2016 blocks so that the average block interval returns to 10 minutes. 210,000 blocks is the subsidy-halving interval, a different schedule.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How does Proof of Work resist Sybil attacks?
option_1: Influence depends on hash power, which is scarce, not on identity count
option_2: Block rewards are paid only to miners who have proven their identity
option_3: Each node must register its IP address with a certificate authority
option_4: Each distinct identity gets exactly one vote on every new block
answer_text: Influence depends on hash power, which is scarce, not on identity count
explanation: Creating more identities costs nothing, but buying more hash power does, so voting weight tracks real cost. One-identity-one-vote is exactly what a Sybil attacker exploits.
concept: Sybil resistance ties influence to a scarce resource.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.2

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the job of Fabric's ordering service?
option_1: Issues X.509 certificates to the member organisations of the channel
option_2: Orders endorsed transactions into blocks without executing chaincode
option_3: Executes chaincode and validates the read-write sets of each transaction
option_4: Stores and disseminates the private data collections of member orgs
answer_text: Orders endorsed transactions into blocks without executing chaincode
explanation: Orderers produce a total order and cut blocks; peers do the execution (endorsement) and validation. Assuming orderers validate transactions is a common error. Certificates come from the CA and are interpreted through the MSP.
concept: Orderer orders only; peers endorse and validate.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What did Ethereum's Merge (September 2022) change?
option_1: Introduced 64 execution shards running in parallel with the main chain
option_2: Moved all smart-contract execution onto Layer-2 rollup networks
option_3: Moved Ethereum from proof of stake back to proof of work mining
option_4: Joined the execution layer to the PoS Beacon Chain, ending PoW mining
answer_text: Joined the execution layer to the PoS Beacon Chain, ending PoW mining
explanation: The Merge swapped PoW consensus for the Beacon Chain's PoS while keeping the existing state and execution layer. Execution sharding was never part of it, and the direction of change was PoW to PoS.
concept: The Merge: PoW → PoS via the Beacon Chain.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Under discretionary access control (DAC), who decides who may access a resource?
option_1: A policy engine evaluating environmental attributes
option_2: The resource's owner
option_3: An administrator, through role assignment only
option_4: A central authority, using security labels
answer_text: The resource's owner
explanation: In DAC the owner grants and revokes rights at discretion, as with Unix permissions or file sharing. That flexibility is also its weakness (permission leakage and Trojan horses). Central labels define MAC.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does a hash pointer contain?
option_1: An encrypted copy of the data that only its owner can decrypt
option_2: The data's location plus a hash of that data
option_3: A digital signature over the data made by the data's owner
option_4: Only the memory address at which the data is currently stored
answer_text: The data's location plus a hash of that data
explanation: Following the pointer retrieves the data and the stored hash lets you check it has not changed. A blockchain is a linked list of hash pointers. A plain pointer gives location only, with no integrity check.
concept: Hash pointer = location + hash of content.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How is a Bitcoin transaction fee determined?
option_1: Sum of inputs minus sum of outputs; the miner collects it
option_2: It is deducted from the previous block's coinbase reward
option_3: It is fixed by protocol at 0.0001 BTC per transaction
option_4: It is a separate output paid to a protocol fee address
answer_text: Sum of inputs minus sum of outputs; the miner collects it
explanation: Any value not assigned to outputs is implicitly the fee, which the miner claims in the coinbase transaction. There is no fee address or fixed protocol fee; fees are set by the market, usually per virtual byte.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.3

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which description matches Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS)?
option_1: Token holders vote to elect a small set of block producers
option_2: Every holder produces blocks in direct proportion to stake
option_3: Validators burn coins to earn the right to produce blocks
option_4: Holders lease their stake to block generators while keeping ownership
answer_text: Token holders vote to elect a small set of block producers
explanation: DPoS (as in EOS, with about 21 producers) concentrates production in elected delegates for speed. The risks are collusion and voter apathy. Leasing stake without giving up ownership describes LPoS.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.8

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Bitcoin's ECDSA signatures are defined over which elliptic curve?
option_1: secp256r1 (NIST P-256)
option_3: Curve25519
option_4: secp256k1
answer_text: secp256k1
explanation: Bitcoin chose the Koblitz curve secp256k1. P-256 (secp256r1) is the NIST curve used widely in TLS, which makes it the tempting wrong answer.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does a CoinJoin transaction achieve?
option_1: Hides the sender's IP address by routing through onion relays
option_2: Encrypts transaction amounts using homomorphic commitments
option_3: Deletes old transactions from the chain once they are fully spent
option_4: Merges several users' inputs into one transaction, hiding who paid whom
answer_text: Merges several users' inputs into one transaction, hiding who paid whom
explanation: Several users co-sign one transaction with equal-value outputs, which breaks the input-output link analysts rely on. Hiding amounts (confidential transactions) and hiding IP addresses (Tor) are separate techniques.
concept: CoinJoin = collaborative mixing in a single transaction.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.6

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An ideal hash has a 20-bit output. An attacker hashes Q = 2^20 random inputs looking for a preimage of one given digest. What is the approximate success probability?
option_2: 100%, because 2^20 inputs cover the whole output space
option_3: About 63% (1 − 1/e)
option_4: About 39%
answer_text: About 63% (1 − 1/e)
explanation: P = 1 − (1 − 1/M)^Q with Q = M gives ≈ 1 − e^(−1) ≈ 0.632. Random inputs can repeat outputs, so trying M of them does not guarantee covering all M values.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: The SHA-256 digests of 'hello' and 'hellp' (one character changed) were computed with Python's hashlib and compared bit by bit. Which result was observed?
option_1: 8 bits differ, one byte's worth
option_2: 1 bit differs, since one character changed
option_3: All 256 bits differ
option_4: 131 of 256 bits differ, close to half
answer_text: 131 of 256 bits differ, close to half
explanation: The avalanche effect means a small input change flips roughly half the output bits; the measured Hamming distance is 131. Assuming the digest changes in proportion to the input is the misconception avalanche design rules out. Flipping every bit would be just as predictable as flipping none.
concept: Avalanche: a 1-bit change flips about 50% of output bits.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A block header's SHA-256 digest begins 0x000039af... (computed with hashlib). How many leading zero bits does it have?
explanation: The four leading hex zeros give 16 zero bits, and the next hex digit 3 is 0011, adding two more, for 18. Stopping at 16 counts only the zero nibbles.
concept: Each leading hex 0 = 4 zero bits; check the next nibble too.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A miner controls 10% of the network hash rate and Bitcoin produces about 144 blocks per day. How many blocks per day should the miner expect?
explanation: The expected share of blocks equals the share of hash rate: 0.10 × 144 = 14.4 per day. Actual counts vary because block discovery is a Poisson process.
concept: Expected blocks = hash-rate share × blocks per period.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A PBFT cluster has 10 replicas. What is the maximum number of Byzantine replicas it can tolerate?
explanation: f = ⌊(n − 1)/3⌋ = ⌊9/3⌋ = 3. The answer 4 comes from the crash-fault formula ⌊(n − 1)/2⌋, which does not hold when faulty nodes can lie.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An attacker holds 25% of the hash power and the merchant waits 6 confirmations. Using the simplified model P = (q/p)^z, what is the catch-up probability?
option_4: 25%, independent of confirmations
explanation: q/p = 0.25/0.75 = 1/3 and (1/3)^6 = 1/729 ≈ 0.14%. The whitepaper's Poisson-refined value is higher (about 5%) because the attacker mines in secret while the merchant waits. Using q instead of q/p understates the risk.
concept: Use the ratio q/p, not q, in the catch-up formula.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.2 & ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A toy Merkle tree uses H(x, y) = (3x + y) mod 17 for every internal node (left child x, right child y). The leaf hashes, left to right, are 2, 5, 7 and 11. What is the root?
explanation: Level 1: H(2,5) = 11 and H(7,11) = 32 mod 17 = 15; root = H(11,15) = 48 mod 17 = 14. Swapping the children gives H(15,11) = 5, which shows why child order matters. 8 is the leaf sum mod 17, and 11 is only the left internal node.
concept: Merkle root: hash pairs bottom-up, keeping left/right order.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Two transactions in the mempool spend the same UTXO to different recipients. A miner includes the first in a block. What happens to the second?
option_1: Both confirm and the sender's balance goes negative
option_2: The miner splits the output between the two recipients
option_3: It becomes invalid, because its input is no longer unspent
option_4: It waits and confirms in the next block
answer_text: It becomes invalid, because its input is no longer unspent
explanation: Once the output is spent on chain it leaves the UTXO set, so any transaction referencing it fails validation everywhere. Bitcoin has no balances that could go negative; each output is spent whole, exactly once.
concept: A UTXO can be spent only once; conflicts are invalid.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.3

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Policy OR(AND('A.member','B.member'), AND('A.member','C.member')). A transaction carries endorsements from B and C. Is the policy satisfied?
option_1: No, but only because B and C belong to different channels
option_2: No: both branches require A
option_3: Yes: each AND branch is half satisfied
option_4: Yes: two of the three organisations signed
answer_text: No: both branches require A
explanation: Each OR branch is an AND that needs A, and A did not endorse, so neither branch holds. Counting signatures out of three would be an OutOf(2, …) policy, which this is not.
concept: Evaluate nested AND/OR exactly; there is no partial credit.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A channel has 5 organisations and uses the default lifecycle endorsement policy (MAJORITY). Two organisations have approved a chaincode definition. Can it be committed?
option_1: Yes: under ANY, 2 of 5 approvals is enough
option_2: No: a majority of 5 needs 3 approvals
option_3: Yes: only the organisation that installed the package must approve
option_4: No: all 5 organisations must approve
answer_text: No: a majority of 5 needs 3 approvals
explanation: MAJORITY means more than half of the channel's organisations, so ⌊5/2⌋ + 1 = 3. checkcommitreadiness would show only two approvals. Installing a package on peers is separate from approving the definition.
concept: Fabric 2.x lifecycle: default MAJORITY of orgs must approve.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Under the Biba integrity model, a Medium-integrity subject tries (i) to read a Low-integrity object and (ii) to write a High-integrity object. What is the result?
option_1: Both are denied: no read down and no write up
option_2: The read is allowed and the write is denied
option_3: The read is denied and the write is allowed
option_4: Both are allowed
answer_text: Both are denied: no read down and no write up
explanation: Biba protects integrity: reading Low data could contaminate the subject, and writing upward could corrupt trusted data. It is the dual of Bell–LaPadula, which is why people who memorised BLP get the directions reversed.
concept: Biba (integrity): no read down, no write up.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Roles form a hierarchy: Senior Manager inherits from Manager, which inherits from Employee. Directly assigned permissions are Employee {view}, Manager {approve}, Senior Manager {sign}. What are a Manager's effective permissions?
option_1: {view, approve, sign}
option_2: {view, approve}
option_3: {view}
option_4: {approve}
answer_text: {view, approve}
explanation: In hierarchical RBAC a senior role inherits its juniors' permissions, so Manager gets its own approve plus Employee's view. Inheritance flows upward only, so Manager does not get the Senior Manager's sign.
concept: Hierarchical RBAC: senior roles inherit junior permissions.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Key K holds the committed value 7. In a single invocation, chaincode calls PutState(K, 10) and then GetState(K). What does GetState return?
option_1: 10, the value just written by PutState
option_2: An error, because K was modified in this transaction
option_3: An empty value, since K is locked during the transaction
option_4: 7, because writes take effect only at commit
answer_text: 7, because writes take effect only at commit
explanation: During simulation, writes go only to the write set; reads come from committed world state, so Fabric does not offer read-your-writes. Developers who expect 10 should keep the new value in a local variable.
concept: No read-your-writes within a Fabric transaction.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: About 35% of all staked ETH goes offline at once. What is the effect?
option_1: The offline validators are slashed immediately for being absent
option_2: Finality continues normally because a majority is still online
option_3: The chain halts completely and no new blocks are produced
option_4: Blocks continue, but finality stalls: 2/3 of stake is unreachable
answer_text: Blocks continue, but finality stalls: 2/3 of stake is unreachable
explanation: Finality needs at least 2/3 of stake, and with over 1/3 offline only 65% remains, so justification fails while LMD-GHOST keeps extending the chain. The inactivity leak gradually drains offline stake until finality resumes; that is a penalty, not slashing, which applies only to equivocation.
concept: > 1/3 stake offline stalls finality, not block production.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: During a network partition, Bitcoin miners on both sides keep extending their own chains, and one branch is discarded after the partition heals. Which CAP trade-off does this show?
option_1: Achieves consistency, availability and partition tolerance simultaneously
option_2: Favours consistency, halting the minority side until the partition heals
option_3: Favours availability; consistency returns via reorg to the heaviest chain
option_4: Sidesteps the trade-off, since PoW chains are immune to partitions
answer_text: Favours availability; consistency returns via reorg to the heaviest chain
explanation: Both sides stay available and accept transactions, so consistency is temporarily lost and restored when the lighter branch is orphaned. Halting the minority side is how BFT-style, consistency-first systems behave, not longest-chain systems.
concept: Longest-chain consensus is AP with probabilistic finality.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.2

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An ordering service must keep working with one malicious orderer and, at the same time, one crashed orderer. Which design is the minimum that meets this?
option_1: Raft ordering with 7 nodes (f = 3 crashes)
option_2: Raft ordering with 5 nodes (f = 2 crashes)
option_3: BFT ordering with 4 nodes (f = 1)
option_4: BFT ordering with at least 7 nodes (f = 2)
answer_text: BFT ordering with at least 7 nodes (f = 2)
explanation: A crashed node also counts against the fault budget, so f = 2 and BFT needs 3f + 1 = 7. Raft of any size tolerates crashes only, and a single lying leader can break it. Four BFT nodes cover only one fault.
concept: Count all simultaneous faults; Byzantine needs 3f+1.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An attacker controls 10% of the hash power. Using the whitepaper's Poisson catch-up model, what is the smallest number of confirmations that brings success below 0.1%?
explanation: For q = 0.1 the model gives about 0.35% at z = 4 and 0.091% at z = 5, so 5 is the first value below 0.1%. Six is the popular rule of thumb, but it overshoots this target (0.024%).
concept: Pick z from the Poisson catch-up table for a target risk.
source: Bitcoin whitepaper (2008), §11

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which check sequence correctly implements ReceiveBatch, where only the intended recipient may mark an in-transit batch as received?
option_1: Set RECEIVED and PutState, relying on the endorsement policy to reject wrong callers
option_2: Check the caller holds any valid certificate from a channel MSP; set RECEIVED; PutState
option_3: Read batch; require IN_TRANSIT; require caller MSP = intended recipient; set RECEIVED; PutState
option_4: Require status QA_RELEASED; require caller = current owner; set RECEIVED; PutState
answer_text: Read batch; require IN_TRANSIT; require caller MSP = intended recipient; set RECEIVED; PutState
explanation: The function must validate the state transition and authorise the caller before writing, following read, authenticate, authorise, validate, write. Endorsement policies decide which peers sign, not which client may call. Any valid certificate is authentication only, and QA_RELEASED is the wrong source state.
concept: Chaincode pattern: read → authN → authZ → validate → write.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why is a blockchain described as tamper-evident?
option_1: A central authority signs each block before nodes will accept it
option_2: Every block is encrypted with the private key of the miner who made it
option_3: Nodes automatically delete altered blocks by checking their timestamps
option_4: Editing a block changes its hash, breaking every later block's link
answer_text: Editing a block changes its hash, breaking every later block's link
explanation: Because each header embeds the previous header's hash, an edit cascades into mismatches all the way to the tip, which any node can detect. Blocks are hashed and the transactions in them signed; they are not encrypted, and no central signer is needed.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the avalanche effect in a cryptographic hash function?
option_1: The output length grows with the length of the input
option_2: A one-bit input change flips about half the output bits
option_3: Similar inputs produce similar, nearby digests
option_4: Hashing time grows exponentially with the input size
answer_text: A one-bit input change flips about half the output bits
explanation: Avalanche makes the outputs of related inputs look unrelated, so attackers cannot work toward a target digest step by step. 'Similar inputs give similar digests' is the opposite, and it is how non-cryptographic locality-sensitive hashes behave.
concept: Avalanche: small change in → about 50% bits change out.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What are SHA-1's digest size and compression structure?
option_1: 160-bit digest; 80 steps arranged as 4 rounds of 20
option_2: 128-bit digest; 64 steps arranged as 4 rounds of 16
option_3: 160-bit digest; 64 steps arranged as 4 rounds of 16
option_4: 256-bit digest; 64 rounds
answer_text: 160-bit digest; 80 steps arranged as 4 rounds of 20
explanation: SHA-1 expands each 512-bit block to 80 words and runs 4 × 20 steps over five 32-bit buffers, giving 160 bits. The 128-bit, 4 × 16 structure is MD5.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How often does the Bitcoin block subsidy halve?
option_1: Every 2016 blocks
option_2: Every 52,560 blocks
option_3: Every 210,000 blocks
option_4: Every 100,000 blocks
answer_text: Every 210,000 blocks
explanation: Halving every 210,000 blocks (about four years) caps total issuance near 21 million BTC. 2016 blocks is the difficulty retarget period.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the minimum cluster size for Raft to tolerate f crash faults?
option_1: 2f + 1 nodes
option_2: 4f nodes
option_3: 3f + 1 nodes
option_4: f + 1 nodes
answer_text: 2f + 1 nodes
explanation: Raft needs a majority to elect a leader and commit entries, so f failures leave f + 1 of 2f + 1 nodes, still a majority. 3f + 1 is the Byzantine bound, which is stricter because faulty nodes may lie.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does a Fabric channel provide?
option_1: A subset of data inside a ledger, with only its hash on chain
option_2: An encrypted link between the client and the orderer only
option_3: A chaincode namespace on a ledger shared by every organisation
option_4: A separate ledger shared only by its member organisations
answer_text: A separate ledger shared only by its member organisations
explanation: Each channel has its own blockchain, world state and membership, so non-members never receive its blocks. Keeping a subset of data private within one ledger, with only a hash on chain, describes a private data collection.
concept: Channel = separate ledger; PDC = private subset within a channel.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which sequence is the Fabric 2.x chaincode lifecycle?
option_1: package → install → approve for my org → commit → invoke
option_2: approve for my org → package → commit → install → invoke
option_3: package → instantiate → install → invoke
option_4: commit → approve for my org → install → package → invoke
answer_text: package → install → approve for my org → commit → invoke
explanation: Fabric 2.x moved to decentralised governance: each organisation installs the package and approves the definition, then one commit activates it on the channel. install → instantiate is the deprecated Fabric 1.x flow found in older books.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Under mandatory access control (MAC), what are access decisions based on?
option_1: The discretion of the resource's owner, who may grant rights to others
option_2: Membership of roles defined by the system administrator
option_3: Access lists that each individual user maintains for their own files
option_4: Central security labels and clearances that owners cannot override
answer_text: Central security labels and clearances that owners cannot override
explanation: MAC enforces a system-wide policy, for example military classifications, where users cannot pass rights to others. The owner's discretion defines DAC, which is the opposite design choice.
concept: MAC: central labels; owners cannot change policy.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is Proof of Burn (PoB)?
option_1: Spending electricity on repeated hash computations to find a nonce
option_2: Locking coins as validator stake that can later be slashed
option_3: Destroying coins provably (unspendable address) to earn mining rights
option_4: Locking coins inside a trusted execution environment for a period
answer_text: Destroying coins provably (unspendable address) to earn mining rights
explanation: Burning gives up value permanently as a costly signal, and the right to mine grows with the amount burned. Stake in PoS can be recovered or slashed, which differs from irreversible destruction.
concept: PoB = burn coins to an unspendable address for mining rights.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.8

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An Ethereum validator signs two different blocks for the same slot. What is the consequence?
option_1: It loses that slot's reward only, as an inactivity penalty
option_2: It is slashed: part of its stake is burned and it is exited
option_3: Nothing, because the fork-choice rule simply picks one block
option_4: Its signing key is revoked by a central certificate authority
answer_text: It is slashed: part of its stake is burned and it is exited
explanation: A double proposal is provable equivocation, which is a slashable offence. Inactivity penalties are for being offline and are far milder. Ethereum has no certificate authority.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which statement about permissionless and permissioned blockchains is correct?
option_1: Permissioned chains cannot run smart contracts or chaincode of any kind
option_2: Permissionless chains require identity checks before any node may join
option_3: Permissioned chains must use Proof of Work to order their transactions
option_4: Permissioned chains admit only identified members; identity stops Sybils
answer_text: Permissioned chains admit only identified members; identity stops Sybils
explanation: When membership is controlled through PKI, identity itself defeats Sybil attacks, so costly PoW or PoS is unnecessary. Fabric is permissioned and runs chaincode, which refutes the smart-contract claim.
concept: Permissioned = known identities; permissionless = open entry, economic security.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain, decentralization chapter

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What do Zerocash-style shielded transactions hide?
option_1: Sender, receiver and amount, with zero-knowledge proofs of validity
option_2: Only the amount, while the sender and receiver addresses stay public
option_3: Only the sender's IP address, using onion routing at the network layer
option_4: Nothing; shielded transactions only compress the transaction data
answer_text: Sender, receiver and amount, with zero-knowledge proofs of validity
explanation: zk-SNARKs prove that inputs exist, are unspent and balance the outputs without revealing them. That goes further than mixing, which only obscures links among public data.
concept: Zero-knowledge proofs give validity without disclosure.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.6

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How many distinct functions h: X → Y exist when |X| = 3 and |Y| = 4?
explanation: Each of the 3 inputs can map to any of 4 outputs independently, giving 4^3 = 64. Reversing the base and exponent (3^4 = 81) counts functions from Y to X, a common slip with hash families.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A toy hash is h(x) = (x + 1) mod 10. Which input collides with x = 23?
explanation: h(23) = 24 mod 10 = 4 and h(33) = 34 mod 10 = 4, a collision. 24 and 34 collide with each other (both 5) but not with 23. The pigeonhole principle forces such collisions when the domain is larger than the range.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A Bitcoin block has 5 transactions. When a level has an odd number of nodes, the last one is duplicated. How many internal hash computations build the tree from the 5 transaction hashes to the root?
explanation: 5 → 3 parents (the 5th is paired with itself), 3 → 2, 2 → 1, so 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Counting n − 1 = 4 assumes a perfect binary tree with no duplication.
concept: Odd levels duplicate the last node in Bitcoin's Merkle tree.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An SPV (light) client wants to verify that a transaction is in a block with 16 transactions. What must it obtain?
option_1: 4 sibling hashes plus the header holding the Merkle root
option_2: 8 sibling hashes, one for each pair of transactions
option_3: All 16 transaction hashes from the block's full body
option_4: The Merkle root alone, taken from any connected peer
answer_text: 4 sibling hashes plus the header holding the Merkle root
explanation: log2 16 = 4 siblings let the client recompute the root, which it compares with the root in a header it trusts through proof of work. The root alone proves nothing about any particular transaction.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: The last 2016 blocks took only 3 days instead of 14. By what factor does Bitcoin raise the difficulty?
option_1: ×4.67 (the raw factor, applied in full)
option_2: ×0.25 (the lower bound of the clamp)
option_3: ×0.21 (actual time ÷ expected time)
option_4: ×4 (the raw 4.67 is clamped)
answer_text: ×4 (the raw 4.67 is clamped)
explanation: The raw factor is 14/3 ≈ 4.67, but each adjustment is clamped to between ¼ and 4, so the difficulty rises ×4. 0.21 inverts the ratio, and ×0.25 is the lower clamp, used when blocks are far too slow.
concept: Retarget clamp limits each change to ×¼…×4.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Blocks arrive as a Poisson process averaging one per 10 minutes. What is the probability that no block is found in a 30-minute window?
option_2: 0%, because three blocks always arrive in 30 minutes
option_3: About 33%
option_4: About 5.0% (e^−3)
answer_text: About 5.0% (e^−3)
explanation: With rate λ = 3 blocks per 30 minutes, P(0) = e^(−3) ≈ 0.0498. The 10-minute figure is an average, not a schedule, so long gaps do happen.
concept: Block arrivals are Poisson; P(no block in t) = e^(−t/600 s).
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A transaction is 250 virtual bytes and the market fee rate is 20 sat/vB. What fee should it pay?
explanation: 250 × 20 = 5,000 sat, and with 10^8 sat per BTC that is 0.00005 BTC. The other options shift the decimal point by one or more places, which is the usual unit error.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.3

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In a BFT system with n = 3f + 1 replicas and quorums of 2f + 1, why are two quorums guaranteed never to commit conflicting values?
option_1: Two quorums are always identical sets of replicas
option_2: Two quorums share ≥ f + 1 replicas, so at least one is honest
option_3: Two quorums share exactly one replica, which might be faulty
option_4: Two quorums share ≥ f replicas, all of which might be faulty
answer_text: Two quorums share ≥ f + 1 replicas, so at least one is honest
explanation: The overlap is 2(2f + 1) − (3f + 1) = f + 1, and with at most f faulty at least one shared replica is honest and will not vote for both values. An overlap of only f could consist entirely of faulty nodes, which is why smaller quorums are unsafe.
concept: Quorum intersection ≥ f+1 guarantees an honest common member.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An attacker controls 60% of the hash power. Which action is within its power?
option_1: Spend coins from any address without knowing the private key
option_2: Raise the 21-million coin cap for every node on the network
option_3: Double-spend its own recent transactions and censor others'
option_4: Make honest nodes accept blocks carrying invalid signatures
answer_text: Double-spend its own recent transactions and censor others'
explanation: Majority hash power controls which valid chain is heaviest, so it can reorganise and exclude transactions. Every node still checks signatures and consensus rules on its own, so invalid blocks are rejected however much work is behind them.
concept: A 51% attacker can reorder and censor but cannot forge.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.2 & ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Policy OutOf(3, 'A.peer', 'B.peer', 'C.peer', 'D.peer', 'E.peer'). A transaction carries endorsements from A's peer and from two different peers of B. Is the policy satisfied?
option_1: Yes: there are three valid peer signatures
option_2: No, because B signing twice is equivocation and B is slashed
option_3: No: only two distinct principals (A.peer and B.peer) are satisfied
option_4: Yes: OutOf counts peers, not principals
answer_text: No: only two distinct principals (A.peer and B.peer) are satisfied
explanation: Each listed principal can be satisfied only once, so a second B signature adds nothing and the count is 2 of the required 3. Counting raw signatures is the trap. Fabric has no slashing; extra signatures are simply ignored.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In Fabric, which component detects that two transactions in the same block try to consume the same asset version?
option_1: The committing peers, during MVCC validation
option_2: The ordering service, while cutting the block
option_3: The certificate authority
option_4: The endorsing peers, during simulation
answer_text: The committing peers, during MVCC validation
explanation: Endorsers simulate each transaction separately against the current state and cannot see the other, and orderers do not inspect read-write sets. Only committing peers, checking transactions in block order, see that the second read version is stale.
concept: Conflicts are caught at validation (MVCC), after ordering.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Bob runs a program from Mallory that copies Bob's secret file into a file Mallory can read. Bob's own rights allow both actions. Which model prevents this leak by design?
option_1: DAC, because Bob owns the secret file and controls its rights
option_2: RBAC, with a single Employee role assigned to everyone
option_3: MAC with Bell–LaPadula's *-property (no write down)
option_4: An ACL on the secret file that lists Bob as its only reader
answer_text: MAC with Bell–LaPadula's *-property (no write down)
explanation: Under DAC a program runs with the user's rights, so a Trojan horse can do anything Bob can, including copying data out. MAC forbids writing high data into a low-level file whatever the user's intentions. The ACL still lets Bob, and therefore the Trojan, read the file.
concept: DAC is vulnerable to Trojan horses; MAC's *-property is not.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Only QA staff may release a batch. How should this be enforced in Fabric chaincode?
option_1: Check in ReleaseBatch that GetMSPID() equals 'ManufacturerMSP'
option_2: Issue role=QA certificate attributes and check them in ReleaseBatch
option_3: Move all QA users onto a separate channel with its own ledger
option_4: Add the QA organisation's peers to the chaincode endorsement policy
answer_text: Issue role=QA certificate attributes and check them in ReleaseBatch
explanation: Certificate attributes carry the role, and the chaincode checks the invoker's role before any write. An endorsement policy decides which peers must sign, not which user may invoke. An MSP check identifies the organisation, not a role within it.
concept: Attribute-based role checks in chaincode implement RBAC.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A designer claims that her deterministic consensus protocol always terminates and stays safe in a fully asynchronous network where one node may crash. Which result refutes this?
option_1: The birthday paradox
option_2: The CAP theorem
option_3: The FLP impossibility result
option_4: The 3f + 1 Byzantine bound
answer_text: The FLP impossibility result
explanation: FLP shows that no deterministic protocol can guarantee both safety and termination under asynchrony with even one crash fault. CAP is tempting, but it concerns availability versus consistency under partitions, not termination with crashes. Real protocols avoid FLP with timing assumptions or randomness.
concept: FLP: async + 1 crash ⇒ no deterministic consensus that always terminates.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.2

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Two ECDSA signatures made with the same private key share the same r value. What can an attacker do?
option_1: Recover only the signer's public key from r
option_2: Nothing, because r is public in every signature
option_3: Recover only the two message hashes being signed
option_4: Solve for the nonce k, then for the private key
answer_text: Solve for the nonce k, then for the private key
explanation: An equal r means the same nonce k was used, so subtracting the two s equations gives k = (z1 − z2)/(s1 − s2) mod n, and the private key follows. Treating r as harmless public data ignores that r is determined by k.
concept: ECDSA nonce reuse leaks the private key.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A hospital network requires that doctors read or update only the records of patients assigned to them, only during their shifts, and only from the hospital network. Which access-control approach best fits?
option_1: Pure RBAC with a single Doctor role covering all patients
option_2: ABAC over role, patient assignment, time and network location
option_3: DAC, with each patient granting rights to chosen doctors
option_4: MAC, with every patient record labelled Top Secret
answer_text: ABAC over role, patient assignment, time and network location
explanation: The rule depends on relationships and context (assignment, shift, location), which attributes express directly. A single Doctor role gives every doctor access to every patient, violating least privilege. DAC and MAC have no natural way to express time or location conditions.
concept: Use ABAC when decisions depend on context and relationships.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which assessment of the claim 'higher difficulty means a more secure PoW chain' is most accurate?
option_1: Partly true: it tracks hash rate, but a >50% pool wins at any difficulty
option_2: True: doubling difficulty doubles the confirmations a merchant needs
option_3: False: difficulty has no relation to the network's total hash rate
option_4: True: an attacker must solve a harder puzzle per block than honest miners do
answer_text: Partly true: it tracks hash rate, but a >50% pool wins at any difficulty
explanation: Difficulty tracks the total hash rate, so it raises the cost of an outside attack. It says nothing about concentration in pools or ASIC owners, or about network topology. Attackers face the same per-block puzzle as everyone else; their advantage comes from their share of the hash power.
concept: Difficulty ≠ security; distribution of hash power matters.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Three organisations want a Raft ordering service that keeps running if any one entire organisation goes offline. Which deployment achieves this?
option_1: 2 orgs × 2 orderers each (4 nodes)
option_2: 3 orgs × 1 orderer each (3 nodes)
option_3: 2 orgs hosting 3 and 2 orderers (5 nodes)
option_4: 1 org hosting all 5 orderers
answer_text: 3 orgs × 1 orderer each (3 nodes)
explanation: With one node per organisation, losing an organisation leaves 2 of 3, still a majority. With 2 + 2, losing either organisation leaves 2 of 4, not a majority. With 3 + 2, losing the 3-node organisation leaves 2 of 5, and a single host is a single point of failure.
concept: Place Raft nodes so that losing any failure domain keeps a majority.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How does a blockchain relate to a distributed ledger?
option_1: A blockchain is one kind of DLT; DAG-based ledgers are another
option_2: Every distributed ledger, by definition, requires mining
option_3: The two terms are exact synonyms for the same data structure
option_4: A blockchain is a centralised variant of a distributed ledger
answer_text: A blockchain is one kind of DLT; DAG-based ledgers are another
explanation: A distributed ledger is any replicated record kept under shared rules. A blockchain specifically links blocks by hashes, while IOTA's Tangle is a DAG. Mining is only one way to reach consensus, and permissioned ledgers do not mine at all.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the key security property of the Merkle–Damgård (iterated) construction?
option_1: The output length doubles with each additional 512-bit block that is processed
option_2: It can hash only messages of one fixed, predefined length
option_3: It needs a secret key, so it works as a MAC by construction
option_4: A collision-resistant compression function gives a collision-resistant hash
answer_text: A collision-resistant compression function gives a collision-resistant hash
explanation: The construction pads the message, appends its length and chains a fixed-size compression function, so security reduces to that function. MD5 and SHA-1 both use it. A keyed construction would be a MAC, which is a different primitive.
concept: MD construction: collision resistance of compression ⇒ of the hash.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How large is a Merkle proof of membership for a tree with n leaves?
option_2: O(n)
option_3: O(n log n)
option_4: O(log n)
answer_text: O(log n)
explanation: The proof carries one sibling hash per tree level, and a balanced binary tree has log2 n levels. O(n) would mean sending every transaction, which is what light clients avoid.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What do miners vary while searching for a valid block?
option_1: The nonce, then extra-nonce or timestamp when nonces run out
option_2: The previous block hash, until a lower hash is found
option_3: The signatures inside transactions, re-signing each attempt
option_4: The difficulty bits, lowering them until a hash qualifies
answer_text: The nonce, then extra-nonce or timestamp when nonces run out
explanation: Changing the nonce (or the extra-nonce in the coinbase, which changes the Merkle root) produces new header hashes to test. The previous hash and difficulty bits are fixed by consensus, and changing them would make the block invalid.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does the agreement property of consensus require?
option_1: Each node decides at most once
option_2: A decided value must satisfy the protocol's validity rules
option_3: Every honest node eventually decides
option_4: No two honest nodes decide different values
answer_text: No two honest nodes decide different values
explanation: Agreement concerns consistency between nodes. Deciding at most once is integrity, satisfying the rules is validity, and eventually deciding is termination (liveness).
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.2

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the world state in Hyperledger Fabric?
option_1: A key-value DB of latest values, rebuildable from the chain
option_2: The ordering service's Raft log of consensus entries
option_3: An immutable copy of every block header since genesis
option_4: A signed list of every member certificate on the channel
answer_text: A key-value DB of latest values, rebuildable from the chain
explanation: The ledger has two parts: the immutable block history and the world state, a cache of current values for fast queries. Replaying the valid transactions in the chain regenerates the world state, so the state is derived data, not the record of truth.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does a Fabric endorsement policy specify?
option_1: Which certificate authority issues the members' certificates
option_2: Which orgs' peers must sign a transaction's simulation results
option_3: Which users may join the channel and read its ledger
option_4: How and when the ordering service cuts new blocks
answer_text: Which orgs' peers must sign a transaction's simulation results
explanation: Committing peers check endorsements against this policy during validation (VSCC). Channel membership and block-cutting parameters are set in channel configuration, not in the chaincode endorsement policy.
concept: Endorsement policy = required signers per chaincode.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does the principle of least privilege require in an RBAC design?
option_1: Each role gets only the permissions its tasks need
option_2: Administrators get every permission to reduce support tickets
option_3: Permissions are assigned directly to users
option_4: Users choose their own roles at login
answer_text: Each role gets only the permissions its tasks need
explanation: Least privilege limits the damage a compromised or careless account can cause. Assigning permissions directly to users bypasses roles altogether and recreates the management problem RBAC solves.
concept: Least privilege: minimal permissions per role.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is a coinbase transaction?
option_1: A transfer of coins out of an exchange's hot wallet to a user
option_2: The first transaction made by each new user to set up and fund a fresh wallet
option_3: A refund of transaction fees from the miner back to the senders
option_4: The block's first tx: no real inputs; pays subsidy plus fees to the miner
answer_text: The block's first tx: no real inputs; pays subsidy plus fees to the miner
explanation: The coinbase creates new coins under the subsidy schedule and collects all fees in the block. Its outputs cannot be spent for 100 blocks (coinbase maturity) in case of reorganisation. The name has nothing to do with the exchange of the same name.
concept: Coinbase = miner's reward transaction with no real inputs.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.3

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the minimum stake needed to activate an Ethereum validator?
option_1: 32 ETH
option_2: 64 ETH
option_3: 16 ETH
option_4: 1 ETH
answer_text: 32 ETH
explanation: A validator activates with 32 ETH deposited to the deposit contract. Smaller holders join through staking pools, which concentrate stake, one of PoS's decentralisation risks.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the nothing-at-stake problem in naive proof of stake?
option_1: Validators run out of electricity during long epochs of production
option_2: Validators can back competing forks at no cost, since signing is cheap
option_3: Blocks can never be finalized because stake keeps changing
option_4: Staked coins cannot be transferred, so liquidity disappears
answer_text: Validators can back competing forks at no cost, since signing is cheap
explanation: Without a penalty, backing every fork is the dominant strategy, which weakens convergence. Slashing makes provable equivocation costly. Electricity cost is PoW's problem, not PoS's.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.8

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: From what is a Bitcoin P2PKH address derived?
option_1: The private key directly, encoded in Base58 with a checksum
option_2: The hash of the genesis block combined with a wallet index
option_3: A hash of the public key (SHA-256 then RIPEMD-160)
option_4: The user's legal name combined with a random nonce
answer_text: A hash of the public key (SHA-256 then RIPEMD-160)
explanation: Hashing the public key shortens the address and hides the key until it is first spent from. Deriving an address directly from the private key would expose it, and identity data plays no part.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An MD5 input is exactly 448 bits long. How many padding bits are added, and what is the final length?
option_1: 0 padding bits; 512 bits in total
option_2: 448 padding bits; 960 bits in total
option_3: 64 padding bits; 512 bits in total
option_4: 512 padding bits; 1024 bits in total
answer_text: 512 padding bits; 1024 bits in total
explanation: Padding is always added: a message already at 448 mod 512 still needs at least the single 1 bit, so a full 512 bits is added to reach the next 448 (960), plus the 64-bit length gives 1024. Zero padding is the trap, because the 1 bit cannot be omitted.
concept: MD5 padding is 1–512 bits, never zero.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Approximately how many queries give a 50% chance of a collision on a 40-bit digest?
option_1: About 1.1 × 10^12 (2^40, the full space)
option_2: About 5.5 × 10^11 (2^39, half the space)
option_3: About 47 (1.17 × 40 digest bits)
explanation: With M = 2^40, √M = 2^20 ≈ 1.05 × 10^6, and multiplying by 1.17 gives about 1.23 × 10^6, which an ordinary laptop can manage. 2^40 is the cost of a preimage attack, not a collision.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A system needs 128-bit security against collision attacks. What is the minimum digest length?
option_1: 192 bits
option_2: 256 bits
option_3: 512 bits
option_4: 128 bits
answer_text: 256 bits
explanation: Birthday attacks find collisions in about 2^(n/2) work, so n/2 ≥ 128 gives n ≥ 256. A 128-bit digest such as MD5 offers only 64-bit collision security.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A puzzle requires 20 leading zero bits in the hash. A device computes 10^6 hashes per second. What is the expected time to solve it?
option_1: About 20 microseconds
option_2: About 1.05 seconds
option_3: About 1,048 seconds
option_4: About 0.5 seconds
answer_text: About 1.05 seconds
explanation: Expected work is 2^20 = 1,048,576 hashes, and at 10^6 per second that takes about 1.05 s. Each additional zero bit doubles the work.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the Bitcoin block subsidy at block height 840,000?
option_3: 6.25 BTC
option_4: 12.5 BTC
explanation: 840,000 / 210,000 = 4 halvings, so the subsidy is 50 / 2^4 = 3.125 BTC. 6.25 BTC applied from block 630,000 until just before 840,000.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An attacker has 30% of the hash power and the merchant waits 2 confirmations. What is the simplified catch-up probability (q/p)^z?
explanation: q/p = 0.3/0.7 = 3/7 and (3/7)^2 ≈ 0.184. An 18% double-spend risk shows why two confirmations are too few against a large minority miner.
concept: Catch-up probability (q/p)^z rises sharply as q approaches p.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.2 & ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A PBFT deployment has 4 replicas. How many Byzantine faults can it tolerate, and how large is a quorum?
option_1: f = 0, quorum 4
option_2: f = 1, quorum 2
option_3: f = 1, quorum 3
option_4: f = 2, quorum 3
answer_text: f = 1, quorum 3
explanation: n = 3f + 1 gives f = 1, and the quorum is 2f + 1 = 3. A quorum of 2 would let two quorums overlap only in a possibly faulty node.
concept: n = 4 is the smallest BFT cluster (f = 1).

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: 1,000,000 ETH is staked, all in 32-ETH validators. How many validators is that?
explanation: 1,000,000 / 32 = 31,250. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 32 million.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A channel has 4 organisations and the chaincode uses the default MAJORITY endorsement policy. A transaction is endorsed by Org1 and Org2 only. What happens?
option_1: It passes: 2 of 4 organisations is half, which suffices
option_2: It passes: by default any single endorsement is enough
option_3: It fails: a majority of 4 requires 3 endorsing organisations
option_4: It fails: all 4 organisations must endorse under MAJORITY
answer_text: It fails: a majority of 4 requires 3 endorsing organisations
explanation: MAJORITY means strictly more than half, so ⌊4/2⌋ + 1 = 3, and two organisations is exactly half. Committing peers would flag the transaction ENDORSEMENT_POLICY_FAILURE.
