source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Org1 and Org2 keep a price in a private data collection. Later Org1 discloses the price and its salt to an auditor from Org3. How can the auditor confirm it is the value recorded on the ledger?
option_1: Query Org1's private database directly through a chaincode call
option_2: It cannot: private data collections leave no trace on the ledger
option_3: Hash the disclosed value and salt; compare with the ledger hash
option_4: Ask the ordering service, which keeps a copy of all private data
answer_text: Hash the disclosed value and salt; compare with the ledger hash
explanation: Every channel peer holds the hash of the private write, so a matching hash proves the disclosed value is authentic. Orderers never receive private data, which travels peer to peer by gossip. Salting stops guessing of low-entropy values.
concept: PDC hashes make later disclosure verifiable.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A batch state machine is CREATED → QA_RELEASED → IN_TRANSIT → RECEIVED. TransferBatch changes the owner at dispatch and accepts batches in either QA_RELEASED or IN_TRANSIT. Which part creates a bypass?
option_1: Accepting TransferBatch while the batch is IN_TRANSIT
option_2: Setting status CREATED in CreateBatch
option_3: Allowing ReceiveBatch only by the intended recipient
option_4: Allowing ReleaseBatch only from CREATED
answer_text: Accepting TransferBatch while the batch is IN_TRANSIT
explanation: The new owner can re-transfer an in-transit batch before it is ever received, which skips the RECEIVED step and breaks custody tracking. The fix is to transfer only from QA_RELEASED (or RECEIVED for onward shipping). The other three are correct guards.
concept: Restrict each state transition to its legal source states.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A Unix file owned by alice, group finance, has mode 640. Bob is in finance; Carol is in neither alice's account nor finance. What access do they have?
option_1: Bob can read and write; Carol can read
option_2: Bob can read only; Carol can read
option_3: Bob can read only; Carol has no access
option_4: Bob has no access; Carol can read
answer_text: Bob can read only; Carol has no access
explanation: 640 means owner rw- (6), group r-- (4), others --- (0). Bob gets group read, and Carol falls under 'others' with nothing. This is DAC: alice could change the mode at will.
concept: Unix mode digits: owner/group/other, r=4 w=2 x=1.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Under a dynamic separation-of-duty rule, user U is assigned both Requester and Approver. U submits a purchase request and then, in the same session, tries to approve it. What happens?
option_1: Allowed if the amount is below a set threshold
option_2: Denied: both roles cannot be active in one session
option_3: Allowed, since U is assigned both roles
option_4: Invalid: the assignment itself breaks static SoD
answer_text: Denied: both roles cannot be active in one session
explanation: Dynamic SoD allows holding conflicting roles but forbids activating them together, so U must drop Requester before acting as Approver. Static SoD would have blocked the assignment, but the scenario states the dynamic form.
concept: Dynamic SoD restricts simultaneous role activation.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A transaction spends inputs from addresses A1 and A2 and pays outputs to B and C. What does the common-input-ownership heuristic conclude?
option_1: Nothing; public transactions reveal no links
option_2: B and C are probably controlled by one entity
option_3: A1 and A2 are probably controlled by one entity
option_4: A1 is probably the owner of output B
answer_text: A1 and A2 are probably controlled by one entity
explanation: Signing for several inputs normally requires holding all their keys, so analysts cluster input addresses. CoinJoin deliberately breaks this assumption. The heuristic says nothing directly about outputs.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.6

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which scenario has the least need for a blockchain?
option_1: One company's internal inventory, with a single trusted writer
option_2: Several mutually distrustful banks settling payments
option_3: A cross-border supply chain with no trusted operator
option_4: A public timestamping registry that no single party should control
answer_text: One company's internal inventory, with a single trusted writer
explanation: A blockchain pays off when multiple writers do not trust each other or any intermediary. With one trusted writer, a conventional database with audit logs is cheaper and faster. The other three involve distributed trust.
concept: No multi-party distrust ⇒ no need for a blockchain.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain, decentralization chapter

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A pool with 28% of the hash power wins half of its block races (γ = 1/2) thanks to good network connectivity. Is selfish mining profitable for it?
option_1: No: selfish mining needs more than 50% of the hash power
option_2: Yes, because any pool profits from it whenever γ > 0
option_3: No: the threshold is always 1/3, whatever the value of γ
option_4: Yes: at γ = 1/2 the threshold is 1/4, and 28% exceeds it
answer_text: Yes: at γ = 1/2 the threshold is 1/4, and 28% exceeds it
explanation: Better connectivity lowers the threshold from 1/3 (γ = 0) to 1/4 (γ = 1/2), so 28% becomes profitable. The threshold falls to zero only when γ = 1. That is why tie-breaking and propagation rules are part of the defence.
concept: Selfish-mining threshold falls as γ rises.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Four banks trade in bilateral pairs. Each pair's trade details must be hidden from the other banks, all banks need one common ordered ledger proving that each trade occurred (for netting), and the regulator must see full details. Which design fits?
option_1: A separate channel for each bilateral pair, each including the regulator
option_2: One shared channel without PDCs; chaincode queries filtered by MSP ID
option_3: One shared channel with a single PDC covering all banks and the regulator
option_4: One shared channel, with a PDC per bilateral pair that includes the regulator
answer_text: One shared channel, with a PDC per bilateral pair that includes the regulator
explanation: The shared channel gives a common ordering and the hashes needed for netting, while per-pair PDCs (including the regulator) hide the details from other banks. Separate channels lose the common ledger. Query restrictions still replicate plaintext to every peer, and a PDC covering everyone hides nothing.
concept: Channels separate ledgers; PDCs hide data within a shared ledger.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Manufacturers create batches and QA staff release them, and the same person must never both create and release a batch. Which chaincode design enforces both rules?
option_1: Check only that GetMSPID() equals 'QAMSP' inside ReleaseBatch
option_2: Store CreatedBy; ReleaseBatch requires role=QA and caller ≠ CreatedBy
option_3: Issue each QA user two certificates and require both signatures
option_4: Endorsement policy AND('QA.peer','Mfr.peer') on the ReleaseBatch function
answer_text: Store CreatedBy; ReleaseBatch requires role=QA and caller ≠ CreatedBy
explanation: The role check enforces RBAC and the per-object comparison with the recorded creator enforces separation of duty at the level of individual people. Endorsement policies govern which peers sign, not who invokes. An MSP check cannot tell apart two people in the same organisation.
concept: Combine role checks with object-level SoD in chaincode.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which set lists the core technologies that a blockchain combines?
option_1: A relational database, SQL triggers, hashing and a certificate authority
option_2: Cloud storage, a VPN, firewalls and consensus
option_3: A central database, client-server networking, symmetric encryption and backups
option_4: A distributed ledger, a peer-to-peer network, cryptography and a consensus mechanism
answer_text: A distributed ledger, a peer-to-peer network, cryptography and a consensus mechanism
explanation: Together these remove the need for a trusted intermediary: replication, P2P communication, cryptographic integrity and agreement on order. The other options describe centralised architectures, which is what blockchains are designed to avoid.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Given an input x, it is infeasible to find a different input x′ with h(x′) = h(x). Which property is this?
option_1: Collision resistance
option_2: Preimage resistance (one-wayness)
option_3: Pseudo-randomness of the output
option_4: Second-preimage resistance
answer_text: Second-preimage resistance
explanation: Here the first input is fixed and the attacker must match its digest. Collision resistance lets the attacker choose both inputs. Preimage resistance starts from a digest alone, with no input given.
concept: Second preimage: given x, find x′ ≠ x with the same digest.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An attacker changes one transaction in a confirmed block. What else must change for the block to look consistent?
option_1: The signatures on every transaction in the block must be redone
option_2: Every hash up to the root, hence the header and all later blocks
option_3: Nothing, since the Merkle root ignores transaction contents
option_4: Only that transaction's own hash inside the block body
answer_text: Every hash up to the root, hence the header and all later blocks
explanation: The change propagates up the tree to the root in the header, which changes the block hash and breaks the next block's link, so the attacker must redo the proof of work for all following blocks. Re-signing is not the problem; the hash commitments are.
concept: Merkle + hash chain make edits cascade.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does a smaller PoW target mean?
option_1: Block times become permanently faster than 10 minutes
option_2: Each block may hold more transactions than before
option_3: More hashes expected per block, so higher difficulty
option_4: Fewer hashes expected per block, so lower difficulty
answer_text: More hashes expected per block, so higher difficulty
explanation: Fewer hash values fall below a smaller target, so success per attempt is less likely. Retargeting keeps block times near 10 minutes, so a smaller target does not make blocks permanently slower or faster.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How does a Byzantine fault differ from a crash fault?
option_1: A Byzantine node may lie or equivocate, not merely stop
option_2: Byzantine faults are hardware failures, never software
option_3: A Byzantine node is always offline and never responds
option_4: A crash-faulty node actively sends false messages
answer_text: A Byzantine node may lie or equivocate, not merely stop
explanation: Crash faults are fail-stop: the node halts or drops messages. Byzantine nodes can equivocate or collude, which is why tolerating them costs 3f + 1 nodes instead of 2f + 1.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why does Fabric separate execution, ordering and validation?
option_1: So the orderer can execute chaincode faster than the endorsing peers can
option_2: Parallel endorsement, early non-determinism checks, logic hidden from orderers
option_3: So peers can mine blocks with proof of work between the phases
option_4: To remove the need for endorsement policies on each channel and chaincode
answer_text: Parallel endorsement, early non-determinism checks, logic hidden from orderers
explanation: Execute-order-validate avoids running every contract sequentially on every node, keeps bad chaincode out of consensus, and limits what orderers learn. The orderer still does no execution, and endorsement policies are central to the design.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why must chaincode be deterministic?
option_1: The orderer re-executes every transaction before cutting blocks
option_2: CouchDB rejects any write that it judges non-deterministic
option_3: All endorsers must produce identical results from the same inputs
option_4: Fabric's gas metering requires a predictable execution cost
answer_text: All endorsers must produce identical results from the same inputs
explanation: Endorsements are compared byte for byte, and different read-write sets cannot form one valid transaction. Orderers never execute chaincode, and Fabric has no gas.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does Ethereum's Gasper protocol combine?
option_1: PBFT voting combined with Raft leader election
option_2: PoW and PoS in a hybrid mining scheme
option_3: LMD-GHOST fork choice with Casper FFG finality
option_4: Tangle tip selection combined with periodic checkpoints
answer_text: LMD-GHOST fork choice with Casper FFG finality
explanation: LMD-GHOST uses the latest attestations to pick the head, and Casper FFG justifies and finalizes checkpoints with 2/3 of stake. Hybrid PoW/PoS existed only during the transition before the Merge.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does attribute-based access control (ABAC) base its decisions on?
option_1: Attributes of subject, resource, action and environment
option_2: The subject's assigned role, and nothing else at all
option_3: The resource owner's personal choice alone, case by case
option_4: Security labels and clearances, and nothing else
answer_text: Attributes of subject, resource, action and environment
explanation: ABAC generalises RBAC by treating role as just one attribute alongside time, location or relationships. That supports fine-grained, context-aware rules at the cost of more complex policies.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does spending a standard P2PKH output require?
option_1: The receiver's wallet password, checked by full nodes
option_2: An approval message signed by the miner of the block
option_3: A signature plus a public key whose hash matches the output
option_4: Revealing the private key itself in the unlocking script
answer_text: A signature plus a public key whose hash matches the output
explanation: The unlocking script supplies <sig> <pubKey>; the locking script checks that the key hashes to the stored value and that the signature verifies. The private key never leaves the wallet.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.3

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How does privacy differ from confidentiality?
option_1: Privacy is simply another word for encrypting the data
option_2: Confidentiality applies only to public, permissionless chains
option_3: They are two words for exactly the same security property
option_4: Confidentiality limits disclosure; privacy governs personal-data use
answer_text: Confidentiality limits disclosure; privacy governs personal-data use
explanation: Encrypting data gives confidentiality but does not by itself settle consent, purpose or retention, which privacy rules address. On a ledger, immutable personal data can raise privacy issues even when access to it is restricted.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.6

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How does IOTA's Tangle structure transactions?
option_1: A linear chain of blocks mined with proof of work
option_2: A DAG in which each new transaction approves earlier ones
option_3: A binary Merkle tree whose root is periodically checkpointed
option_4: A ring of elected validators taking turns to sign
answer_text: A DAG in which each new transaction approves earlier ones
explanation: In the Tangle, transactions themselves form a DAG and approve earlier tips. Tip selection and confirmation rules still apply, so it is not consensus-free. That makes it a DLT but not a blockchain.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.8

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A Merkle tree over 8 transactions uses SHA-256, which gives 32-byte hashes. How many bytes of sibling hashes does one membership proof contain?
option_1: 96 bytes
option_2: 24 bytes
option_3: 64 bytes
option_4: 256 bytes
answer_text: 96 bytes
explanation: Depth log2 8 = 3 gives 3 siblings × 32 bytes = 96. 256 bytes would be all 8 leaf hashes, and 24 bytes treats each hash as 8 bytes.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: On a 64-bit digest, roughly how many times more work is a second-preimage attack than a generic collision attack?
option_1: About 2 times
option_2: The same amount of work
option_3: About 64 times
option_4: About 2^32 times
answer_text: About 2^32 times
explanation: A second preimage costs about 2^64 evaluations and a collision about 2^32 (the birthday bound), so the ratio is about 2^32 ≈ 4.3 × 10^9. That gap is why collision resistance is the first property to fail as digests get shorter.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: The last 2016 Bitcoin blocks took 16 days. What is the new difficulty?
option_1: Unchanged
option_2: 0.25 × the old difficulty (the lower clamp)
option_3: 1.143 × the old difficulty (harder)
option_4: 0.875 × the old difficulty (easier)
answer_text: 0.875 × the old difficulty (easier)
explanation: D_new = D_old × 14/16 = 0.875, because slow blocks mean the hash rate fell. 1.143 inverts the ratio, and the ¼ clamp applies only at extreme slowdowns.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A toy chain accepts a block whose SHA-256 hex digest begins with three zeros. What is the expected number of hashes per block?
explanation: Each hex digit is zero with probability 1/16, so three zero digits give (1/16)^3 = 1/4096, and 4,096 hashes are expected. 16,777,216 = 16^6 is the figure for six zero digits.
concept: k leading hex zeros ⇒ 16^k expected hashes.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An attacker sends a payment to a merchant's node and, at the same moment, a conflicting payment to himself toward well-connected miners. The merchant accepts zero confirmations. What is this attack, and what mitigates it?
option_1: A 51% attack; only majority hash power mitigates it
option_2: A race attack; waiting for confirmations mitigates it
option_3: Selfish mining; publishing blocks faster mitigates it
option_4: A Sybil attack; using more IP addresses mitigates it
answer_text: A race attack; waiting for confirmations mitigates it
explanation: The attack exploits the merchant trusting a transaction that is not yet mined, and needs no hash power at all. Once the payment is buried under confirmations, the attacker's conflicting transaction can no longer win without out-mining the network.
concept: 0-conf acceptance is vulnerable to race attacks.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.2 & ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: 900 validators have equal stake. What is the minimum number of attestations needed to justify a checkpoint (at least 2/3 of total stake)?
explanation: 2/3 × 900 = 600, and the protocol accepts exactly two-thirds. 451 is a simple majority, which suffices for fork-choice weight but not for FFG justification.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A PBFT cluster grows from 4 to 6 replicas. How many Byzantine faults does it now tolerate?
option_1: 0, because 6 is not of the form 3f + 1
option_2: 1, unchanged; f = 2 needs 7 replicas
option_3: 2, since every extra pair adds one fault
option_4: 3, half of the six replicas
answer_text: 1, unchanged; f = 2 needs 7 replicas
explanation: f = ⌊(6 − 1)/3⌋ = 1, so the two extra replicas add cost without adding fault tolerance. Sizes of 3f + 1 (4, 7, 10…) are the efficient points.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Tx1 (coinbase) pays 6.25 BTC to A. Tx2 spends Tx1:0 and pays 4 BTC to B (output 0) and 2.24 BTC to A (output 1). Tx3 spends Tx2:0 and pays 3.5 BTC to C (output 0) and 0.49 BTC to B (output 1). Which outputs are unspent after Tx3?
option_1: Only Tx3:0 and Tx3:1, the outputs of the newest tx
option_2: Tx2:0, Tx2:1 and Tx3:0 (three outputs remain)
option_4: Tx1:0, Tx2:1, Tx3:0 and Tx3:1 (four outputs remain)
explanation: Tx1:0 was consumed by Tx2 and Tx2:0 by Tx3; everything else is unspent. The fees are 0.01 BTC in each of Tx2 and Tx3 (0.02 BTC total), which explains why the outputs sum to less than 6.25.
concept: Trace UTXOs by marking each referenced output as spent.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.3

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Policy AND('Reg.member', OutOf(2, 'A.member', 'B.member', 'C.member')). Which set of endorsements satisfies it?
option_1: {Reg, A, C}
option_2: {A, B, C}
option_3: {Reg, B}
option_4: {Reg}
answer_text: {Reg, A, C}
explanation: Reg is mandatory and any two of A, B and C are needed, which {Reg, A, C} provides. {A, B, C} is the tempting choice because it has the most signatures, but it lacks the mandatory Reg.
concept: AND with a mandatory principal plus OutOf for flexibility.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Three of the five nodes in a Raft ordering service crash. What is the effect?
option_1: Ordering continues with the two remaining orderer nodes
option_2: Peers take over ordering until the orderers recover
option_3: Committed blocks are rolled back to the last checkpoint
option_4: Ordering halts (no majority); peers can still serve queries
answer_text: Ordering halts (no majority); peers can still serve queries
explanation: Raft needs 3 of 5 to elect a leader and replicate entries, so no new blocks are cut, which is a loss of liveness. Safety holds and committed blocks stay final. Peers have no ordering role.
concept: Raft: losing the majority stops progress but keeps safety.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A lab invoke returns success from the peer CLI, but a later query still shows the old value. What is the most likely reason?
option_1: The tx failed validation at commit; invoke success meant only endorsement
option_2: Queries are served from the orderer's cache, which lags several blocks behind
option_3: CouchDB must be reindexed before new values become visible
option_4: The chaincode must be re-instantiated after every invoke
answer_text: The tx failed validation at commit; invoke success meant only endorsement
explanation: Endorsement success is not commit success. The client must check the commit status or transaction event to learn whether the transaction was marked VALID. Orderers do not serve queries, and 'instantiate' is Fabric 1.x terminology.
concept: Check commit status; invoke success ≠ business success.
source: Bashir, Mastering Blockchain (Hyperledger chapter; answered in Fabric 2.x terms)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Under Bell–LaPadula with categories, a subject at (Secret, {NUC}) requests read access to an object at (Confidential, {NUC, EUR}). What is the decision?
option_1: Allowed, because the *-property permits reading downward
option_2: Denied: the subject lacks category EUR, so does not dominate
option_3: Denied, because BLP forbids reading a lower level
option_4: Allowed, because Secret is higher than Confidential
answer_text: Denied: the subject lacks category EUR, so does not dominate
explanation: Reading requires dominance in both level and categories: Secret ≥ Confidential holds, but {NUC} ⊉ {NUC, EUR}. Comparing levels alone is the trap. BLP has no 'no read down' rule; that belongs to Biba.
concept: BLP dominance: level ≥ and category superset.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An organisation creates one role for every combination of 10 departments, 5 job functions and 3 locations. How many roles result, and what is the problem?
option_1: 150 roles: role explosion; treat department and location as attributes
option_2: 18 roles, because role dimensions add rather than multiply
option_3: 150 roles, which least privilege requires and which is harmless
option_4: 15 roles, one for each job-function and location pair
answer_text: 150 roles: role explosion; treat department and location as attributes
explanation: Combinations multiply: 10 × 5 × 3 = 150. Maintaining that many roles invites errors and accumulated privilege. Keeping roles for job functions and treating context as attributes avoids the blow-up.
concept: Role explosion arises from encoding context into roles.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Alice wants to send X to Bob so that only Bob can read it and Bob can be sure it came from Alice. Which construction achieves both?
option_1: Encrypt with Alice's private key, then Bob's public key
option_2: Encrypt with Bob's private key, then Alice's public key
option_3: Encrypt once, using only Bob's public key
option_4: Encrypt with Alice's public key, then Bob's private key
answer_text: Encrypt with Alice's private key, then Bob's public key
explanation: The inner private-key operation authenticates Alice, and the outer encryption under Bob's public key gives confidentiality. Bob decrypts with his private key, then checks with Alice's public key. Using only Bob's public key gives confidentiality but no proof of origin.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A PoW network uses 150 TWh per year and processes 400,000 transactions per day. Which statement is correct?
option_1: ≈2.8 kWh/tx, counting only block-validation energy
option_2: ≈1,030 kWh/tx on average, but marginal energy per tx is near zero
option_3: ≈1,030 kWh/tx, which is the marginal energy each tx causes
option_4: ≈375,000 kWh/tx, using daily transactions with yearly energy
answer_text: ≈1,030 kWh/tx on average, but marginal energy per tx is near zero
explanation: 150 × 10^9 kWh / (400,000 × 365) ≈ 1,027 kWh per transaction, an average accounting ratio. Miners hash at the same rate whatever the block contents, so the marginal cost of one transaction is near zero. The other figures come from unit errors.
concept: Energy per tx is an average, not a marginal cost.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A staking operator runs the same validator key on two machines at once for redundancy. How should this be assessed?
option_1: Safe: redundancy avoids inactivity penalties and has no downside
option_2: Safe, as long as both machines sit in the same data centre
option_3: Unsafe: two signers can equivocate and be slashed; use protected failover
option_4: Unsafe only because running two machines doubles the gas costs
answer_text: Unsafe: two signers can equivocate and be slashed; use protected failover
explanation: Two independent signers can produce double proposals or double votes, which are provable and slashed, a far larger loss than the inactivity penalty they were meant to avoid. Location does not matter. Correct redundancy is failover with protection against signing twice.
concept: Never run one validator key on two active machines.

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: You must design a tamper-evident audit log of access-control decisions in a permissioned network, with efficient proof that a given decision was logged. Which design best meets this?
option_1: Encrypt each log entry with AES so that nobody can alter it
option_2: Store an MD5 hash of each entry in the same database table
option_3: Store logs in a database and sign the database file once a year
option_4: Use Merkle leaves and anchor the roots on the ledger; O(log n) proofs
answer_text: Use Merkle leaves and anchor the roots on the ledger; O(log n) proofs
explanation: Anchoring the root on a replicated ledger takes the log's integrity out of any single administrator's hands, and Merkle proofs keep verification cheap. Encryption hides data but does not detect substitution. MD5 hashes stored next to the data can simply be recomputed by whoever alters it.
concept: Anchor Merkle roots on chain for tamper-evident logs.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.1

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A small PoW altcoin's total hash rate is only 30% of what can be rented on a marketplace for the same algorithm. An exchange requires 10 confirmations for deposits. How should this be assessed?
option_1: Only a Sybil attack is possible here, so double spends cannot occur
option_2: Safe: with 10 confirmations, (q/p)^10 is negligible for any attacker
option_3: Safe: an attacker would first need to buy and own the mining hardware
option_4: Weak: renting a majority makes P = 1; confirmations only raise attack cost
answer_text: Weak: renting a majority makes P = 1; confirmations only raise attack cost
explanation: Rentable hash power lets an attacker exceed the honest network, so q > p and the catch-up formula no longer applies; P = 1. Confirmations just lengthen the rental period. This is how real 51% attacks on small chains have happened.
concept: When q ≥ p, no number of confirmations is safe.
source: Narayanan et al., Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies, ch.2 & ch.5

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which property makes it infeasible, given a digest y, to find any input x with h(x) = y?
option_1: Preimage resistance
option_2: Second-preimage resistance
option_3: The avalanche effect
option_4: Collision resistance
answer_text: Preimage resistance
explanation: Preimage resistance (one-wayness) is about inverting a given digest. Second-preimage resistance starts from a given message x, not from a digest.
concept: Preimage resistance = cannot invert a digest.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why must collisions exist for every hash function with a fixed-length output?
option_1: More possible inputs than outputs (pigeonhole)
option_2: Hash functions reuse the same internal constants
option_3: Padding repeats the final block
option_4: Designers add them as trapdoors
answer_text: More possible inputs than outputs (pigeonhole)
explanation: Infinitely many inputs map into a finite set of 2^n digests, so some inputs must share a digest. Collision resistance only means collisions are infeasible to find.
concept: No hash is collision-free; resistance is about finding them.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Adding a single full stop to a sentence changes about half the bits of its SHA-256 digest. What is this called?
option_1: Length extension
option_2: Second-preimage resistance
option_3: The avalanche effect
option_4: Padding sensitivity
answer_text: The avalanche effect
explanation: The avalanche effect means a tiny input change scrambles roughly 50% of output bits. It is a design goal, not one of the formal resistance properties.
concept: Avalanche: one-bit change, about half the output flips.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In the hash family (X, Y, K, H), what characterises an unkeyed hash function such as SHA-256?
explanation: An unkeyed hash is the special case with a single fixed function, so the key set has one element. A keyed family (|K| > 1) is what a MAC uses.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which statement about the hierarchy of hash properties is correct?
option_1: The three properties are fully independent
option_2: Preimage resistance implies collision resistance
option_3: Collision resistance implies second-preimage resistance
option_4: Second-preimage resistance implies collision resistance
answer_text: Collision resistance implies second-preimage resistance
explanation: If you could find a second preimage for some x, you would hold a colliding pair, so a collision-resistant hash must resist second preimages. The converse does not hold.
concept: Collision resistance is the strongest of the three.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why is an unkeyed hash alone insufficient when Mallory controls the only channel?
option_1: She can read the digest and invert it to the message
option_2: She can alter the message and recompute the hash
option_3: Hashes only work on short messages
option_4: Hashes cannot be sent over networks
answer_text: She can alter the message and recompute the hash
explanation: Anyone can compute an unkeyed hash, so an attacker on the channel replaces both message and digest. A MAC fixes this by requiring a secret key.
concept: Unkeyed hashes need an authentic channel for the digest.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which security service does a MAC NOT provide?
option_1: Detection of tampering
option_2: Non-repudiation
option_3: Data-origin authentication
option_4: Data integrity
answer_text: Non-repudiation
explanation: Both parties share the key, so either could have produced a tag and a third party cannot tell which. Integrity and origin authentication are what a MAC does provide.
concept: MAC: integrity and authentication, but no non-repudiation.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In the random oracle model, what does the oracle return when queried twice with the same input?
option_1: The inverse of the first output
option_2: An error on the second query
option_3: A fresh random value each time
option_4: The same value both times
answer_text: The same value both times
explanation: Consistency is part of the model: repeated queries return the stored value. Only new inputs receive a fresh uniform output.
concept: Random oracle: consistent on repeats, uniform on new inputs.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What defines an (epsilon, Q) Las Vegas algorithm?
option_1: At most Q queries, success at least epsilon, never a wrong answer
option_2: Exactly Q queries and always succeeds
option_3: Unlimited queries but may return wrong answers
option_4: Exactly Q queries, success at most epsilon, may answer wrongly
answer_text: At most Q queries, success at least epsilon, never a wrong answer
explanation: A Las Vegas algorithm either returns a correct answer or reports failure. Epsilon bounds its average success probability and Q bounds its oracle queries.
concept: Las Vegas: correct or fail, never wrong.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the output size of SHA-1?
option_1: 160 bits
option_2: 256 bits
option_3: 128 bits
option_4: 224 bits
answer_text: 160 bits
explanation: SHA-0 and SHA-1 both produce 160-bit digests. MD5 gives 128 bits and SHA-256 gives 256 bits.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which standard uses a sponge construction instead of Merkle-Damgård?
option_1: SHA-256
option_2: MD5
option_3: SHA-1
option_4: SHA-3 (Keccak)
answer_text: SHA-3 (Keccak)
explanation: SHA-3 was chosen by open competition in 2015 and uses a sponge, giving a structurally different backup to SHA-2. MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-2 are Merkle-Damgård designs.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In CBC-MAC with IV = 0, what is output as the tag?
option_1: The XOR of all plaintext blocks
option_2: Only the final ciphertext block
option_3: The first ciphertext block
option_4: All ciphertext blocks
answer_text: Only the final ciphertext block
explanation: CBC-MAC encrypts in CBC mode and discards every block except the last. Sending all blocks would be CBC encryption, not a MAC.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In the random oracle model, what is the probability that two distinct inputs hash to the same value if |Y| = M?
explanation: Outputs for distinct inputs are independent and uniform, so the second matches the first with probability 1/M. This independence is what drives the attack bounds.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Using the birthday approximation Q ≈ 1.17√M, about how many hash queries give a 50% chance of a collision for a 40-bit digest?
option_1: About 1.2 million
option_2: About 1.1 trillion
option_3: About 2^39
option_4: About 40 thousand
answer_text: About 1.2 million
explanation: √(2^40) = 2^20 ≈ 1.05 million, times 1.17 gives about 1.2 million. 2^39 would be the order of a preimage search, not a collision search.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A designer needs 128-bit security against collision attacks. What is the minimum digest length?
option_1: 256 bits
option_2: 128 bits
option_3: 512 bits
option_4: 160 bits
answer_text: 256 bits
explanation: Birthday attacks cost 2^(n/2), so n/2 = 128 gives n = 256. A 128-bit digest offers only 64-bit collision security.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: With 30 random people, what is the approximate chance that at least two share a birthday?
option_1: About 30%
option_2: About 8%
option_3: About 70%
option_4: About 97%
answer_text: About 70%
explanation: 1 − ∏(1 − i/365) for i up to 29 is about 0.706. 50% is reached at 23 people and 97% near 50.
concept: Birthday paradox: pairs grow as Q²/2.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why are collision attacks so much cheaper than second-preimage attacks?
option_1: Second preimages require the key
option_2: Collisions need no hash evaluations
option_3: Collisions only need the padding
option_4: Q queries create about Q²/2 candidate pairs
answer_text: Q queries create about Q²/2 candidate pairs
explanation: In a collision search every pair of outputs is a chance to match, so success grows with Q². A second-preimage search must hit one fixed digest, so success grows only with Q.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: For an n-bit ideal hash, roughly how many queries does a preimage attack need for a good chance of success?
option_1: About n^2
option_2: About 2^n
option_3: About 2n
option_4: About 2^(n/2)
answer_text: About 2^n
explanation: Each query hits the target with probability 1/M = 2^-n, so success ≈ Q/M and Q must approach 2^n. 2^(n/2) is the collision bound.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: The toy hash h(x) = (a·x) mod n lets an attacker compute h(x1 + x2) from h(x1) and h(x2). Which requirement fails?
option_1: Fixed output length
option_2: Preimage resistance (one-wayness) against inversion
option_3: No shortcuts (pseudorandom evaluation)
option_4: Determinism
answer_text: No shortcuts (pseudorandom evaluation)
explanation: Linearity gives h(x1 + x2) = h(x1) + h(x2) mod n without knowing a, an algebraic shortcut. Deterministic, fixed-length output is still present, so those are not the failures.
concept: Good hashes are non-linear: no algebraic shortcuts.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An attacker holds Alice's signature on h(x) for contract x and wants a different contract with the same hash. Which property protects Alice?
option_1: Preimage resistance
option_2: Second-preimage resistance
option_3: The avalanche effect
option_4: Collision resistance of the signature scheme
answer_text: Second-preimage resistance
explanation: The attacker starts from a fixed, given message x and needs x' with h(x') = h(x). That is the second-preimage problem; preimage resistance starts from a digest with no message.
concept: Fixed message, find a twin = second preimage.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: With Merkle-Damgård padding (1 bit, zeros, 64-bit length) and 512-bit blocks, how many blocks does a 1,200-bit message occupy?
option_1: 5 blocks
option_2: 3 blocks
option_3: 2 blocks
option_4: 4 blocks
answer_text: 3 blocks
explanation: 1,200 + 1 + 64 = 1,265 bits needs rounding up to 1,536 = 3 × 512. Two blocks (1,024 bits) cannot hold even the message.
concept: Pad = 1, zeros, length; total a multiple of the block size.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: For a 500-bit message, how many zero bits does SHA-1 padding add, using d = (447 − |x|) mod 512?
explanation: (447 − 500) mod 512 = −53 mod 512 = 459. Then 500 + 1 + 459 + 64 = 1,024 bits, exactly two blocks.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why could attackers forge a rogue CA certificate using MD5 in 2008?
option_1: Preimage attacks let them invert the CA's signed digest
option_2: MD5 has no padding step
option_3: MD5 digests are reversible
option_4: Chosen-prefix collisions let two certificates share one digest
answer_text: Chosen-prefix collisions let two certificates share one digest
explanation: Researchers built a benign and a rogue certificate with equal MD5 hashes, so the CA's signature on one was valid for the other. Inversion was never needed; this was a collision attack.
concept: Signatures inherit the hash's collision weaknesses.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What change separates SHA-1 from SHA-0?
option_1: Removal of the length padding
option_2: A sponge construction
option_3: A longer 256-bit output with an extra fifth round
option_4: A one-bit rotation in the message schedule
answer_text: A one-bit rotation in the message schedule
explanation: SHA-1 adds ROTL^1 when expanding 16 words to 80, fixing the flaw that weakened SHA-0. Both keep 160-bit output and Merkle-Damgård padding.
concept: SHA-1 = SHA-0 + 1-bit rotation in the schedule.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which authenticated-encryption composition lets the receiver reject forged packets before decrypting anything?
option_1: MAC-then-Encrypt
option_2: Encrypt-then-MAC
option_3: Encrypt-and-MAC
option_4: Encrypt with CBC-MAC as the cipher
answer_text: Encrypt-then-MAC
explanation: In Encrypt-then-MAC the tag covers the ciphertext, so it can be checked first. MAC-then-Encrypt hides the tag inside the ciphertext, so decryption must come first.
concept: EtM: verify the tag on the ciphertext, then decrypt.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: CBC encryption and CBC-MAC share key K. Mallory replaces c0, c1, c2 with garbage but keeps c3 and the tag. What happens?
option_1: Bob's MAC check passes on corrupted plaintext
option_2: Bob recovers the original plaintext
option_3: Bob's MAC check fails and the packet is discarded
option_4: Decryption raises a padding error
answer_text: Bob's MAC check passes on corrupted plaintext
explanation: Recomputing CBC-MAC over the decrypted blocks reproduces each garbage block and ends at E(D(c3)) = c3, the original tag. The integrity check is defeated.
concept: Never use CBC + CBC-MAC with one key.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which mode safely combines a block cipher's encryption with CBC-MAC, as in WPA2's CCMP?
option_1: CBC encryption with CBC-MAC
option_2: ECB encryption with CBC-MAC
option_3: CBC encryption with no MAC
option_4: CTR encryption with CBC-MAC (CCM)
answer_text: CTR encryption with CBC-MAC (CCM)
explanation: CCM encrypts in counter mode, which does not feed ciphertext into the MAC chain, so any ciphertext change breaks verification. CBC with CBC-MAC under one key is the broken case.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A startup stores passwords as unsalted MD5 because 'MD5 collisions do not matter for passwords'. What is the best critique?
option_1: MD5 is too fast and unsalted hashes allow precomputed lookups
option_2: The claim is correct, so the design is fine
option_3: MD5 collisions let anyone log in with any chosen password
option_4: MD5 digests can be decrypted with the key
answer_text: MD5 is too fast and unsalted hashes allow precomputed lookups
explanation: Collision breaks are indeed not the main risk here, but MD5's speed and the missing salt make dictionary and rainbow-table attacks cheap. Use a salted, slow password hash such as bcrypt or Argon2.
concept: Passwords need salt and a deliberately slow hash.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A ledger uses a 128-bit hash for transaction IDs and argues it gives '128-bit security'. Which assessment is right?
option_1: 128 bits is ample for any use
option_2: Collision security is 256 bits
option_3: Collision security is only about 64 bits, so 256 bits is needed
option_4: Preimage security is only about 64 bits, so 512 bits are needed
answer_text: Collision security is only about 64 bits, so 256 bits is needed
explanation: Birthday attacks find collisions in about 2^64 work for a 128-bit digest. Preimage security stays near 2^128; it is collisions that fall to half the length.
concept: Halve the digest length for collision security.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: You must design integrity for API webhooks sent over HTTPS to many clients. Which design is soundest?
option_1: An MD5 checksum signed with RSA
option_2: SHA-256 digest of the body sent in a header alongside the payload
option_3: CBC-MAC and CBC encryption with one shared key
option_4: HMAC-SHA256 tag with a per-client secret, verified before processing
answer_text: HMAC-SHA256 tag with a per-client secret, verified before processing
explanation: A keyed HMAC with per-client secrets stops forgery and limits damage if one key leaks. An unkeyed digest can be recomputed by anyone, and the other options rely on broken constructions.
concept: Webhook integrity = per-client HMAC, verified first.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Fermat's little theorem states that for prime p and gcd(a, p) = 1:
option_1: a^p ≡ 1 (mod p)
option_2: a^(p−1) ≡ 0 (mod p)
option_3: a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p)
option_4: a^(p+1) ≡ a (mod p)
answer_text: a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p)
explanation: For a not divisible by p, raising to p − 1 gives 1. The corollary a^p ≡ a holds for every a, not a^p ≡ 1.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: When does a modular inverse of a modulo m exist?
option_1: Whenever a < m
option_2: Exactly when gcd(a, m) = 1
option_3: Only when a is prime
option_4: Whenever m is even
answer_text: Exactly when gcd(a, m) = 1
explanation: Bézout gives sa + tm = 1 only when a and m are coprime, and then s is the inverse. Size or primality of a alone do not decide it.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does the extended Euclidean algorithm return beyond the gcd?
option_1: The square root of a mod m
option_2: Integers s, t with s·a + t·m = gcd(a, m)
option_3: The order of a mod m
option_4: The prime factorisation of m, used to test a
answer_text: Integers s, t with s·a + t·m = gcd(a, m)
explanation: Back-substitution expresses the gcd as a linear combination; when it is 1, s is a^−1 mod m. It does not factor numbers.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What condition does the Chinese remainder theorem require of the moduli?
option_1: They are all odd
option_2: They sum to the product
option_3: They are pairwise coprime
option_4: They are all prime
answer_text: They are pairwise coprime
explanation: Pairwise coprime moduli guarantee a unique solution modulo their product. They need not be prime: 4 and 9 work.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why does RSA-CRT make decryption about four times faster?
option_1: It skips the modular exponentiation
option_2: It uses a smaller public exponent
option_3: It avoids computing d
option_4: It works with two half-size moduli p and q
answer_text: It works with two half-size moduli p and q
explanation: Exponentiation cost grows roughly with the cube of modulus size, so two exponentiations mod p and mod q are much cheaper than one mod n. d is still used, reduced mod p − 1 and q − 1.
concept: RSA-CRT: compute mod p and mod q, then combine.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which paper introduced public-key cryptography in 1976?
option_1: Merkle and Hellman's knapsack paper
option_2: Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography'
option_3: Nakamoto's Bitcoin white paper
option_4: Rivest, Shamir and Adleman, 'A Method for Digital Signatures'
answer_text: Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography'
explanation: Diffie and Hellman proposed public-key ideas and key exchange in 1976. RSA followed in 1977 and the knapsack scheme in 1978.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why do real systems use hybrid encryption?
option_1: Symmetric keys need no protection
option_2: Hybrid systems avoid using keys
option_3: Public-key schemes cannot encrypt data longer than one block
option_4: Public-key operations are far slower than symmetric ciphers
answer_text: Public-key operations are far slower than symmetric ciphers
explanation: Public-key cryptography is 100–1,000 times slower, so it is used to agree or wrap a session key and AES encrypts the bulk data. Public-key schemes can encrypt, just inefficiently.
concept: PKC for the key, symmetric for the data.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: To send a message only Bob can read, Alice encrypts with:
option_1: Alice's public key
option_2: Bob's public key
option_3: Alice's private key
option_4: Bob's private key
answer_text: Bob's public key
explanation: Only Bob's private key undoes encryption under his public key, giving confidentiality. Encrypting with Alice's private key gives authentication, not secrecy.
concept: Secrecy: encrypt to the receiver's public key.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Encrypting with the sender's private key provides which service?
option_1: Secrecy and authentication, but no non-repudiation
option_2: Authentication and non-repudiation, but no secrecy
option_3: Both secrecy and authentication
option_4: Neither service
answer_text: Authentication and non-repudiation, but no secrecy
explanation: Anyone with the sender's public key can decrypt, so there is no confidentiality, but only the sender could have produced it. That is the basis of digital signatures.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which algorithm supports encryption, signatures and key exchange?
option_1: DSA
option_2: Diffie–Hellman
option_3: SHA-256
option_4: RSA
answer_text: RSA
explanation: RSA serves all three applications. Diffie–Hellman only exchanges keys and DSA only signs.
concept: RSA covers all three PKC uses.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What distinguishes a trapdoor one-way function from a plain one-way function?
option_1: It has no inverse at all
option_2: Secret information makes inversion easy
option_3: It requires a hash function
option_4: It is hard to compute in both directions
answer_text: Secret information makes inversion easy
explanation: A trapdoor function is easy forward, hard to invert, but easy to invert with the trapdoor. A plain one-way function is hard to invert for everyone.
concept: Trapdoor = one-way except for the key holder.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A sequence is superincreasing when each term:
option_1: Is prime
option_2: Is greater than the term just before it
option_3: Exceeds the sum of all earlier terms
option_4: Is a multiple of the first term
answer_text: Exceeds the sum of all earlier terms
explanation: Superincreasing means a_j > a_1 + … + a_(j−1), which makes greedy subset-sum solving work. Merely increasing is not enough.
concept: Superincreasing: each term > sum of predecessors.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is 128^129 mod 17?
explanation: By Fermat, 128^16 ≡ 1, and 129 = 8·16 + 1, leaving 128 mod 17 = 9. Answering 1 forgets the leftover exponent.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is 2^1000 mod 13?
explanation: 2^12 ≡ 1 and 1000 = 83·12 + 4, so the answer is 2^4 = 16 ≡ 3. 4 is the reduced exponent, not the residue.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Solve x^103 ≡ 4 (mod 11).
concept: Reduce exponent, then test small x.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Solve 3x ≡ 4 (mod 7).
explanation: 3^−1 mod 7 is 5, and 5·4 = 20 ≡ 6. 5 is the inverse itself, not the solution.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is 19^−1 mod 141?
explanation: Euclid gives 1 = 52·19 − 7·141, so 52·19 = 988 = 7·141 + 1. 89 is −52 mod 141, which is the negative of the inverse.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is 13^−1 mod 2436?
explanation: Euclid: 2436 = 187·13 + 5, 13 = 2·5 + 3, 5 = 3 + 2, 3 = 2 + 1, giving 1 = 937·13 − 5·2436. 947 leaves remainder 131, so it is not the inverse.
concept: Always verify: a·a^−1 mod m must be 1.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Solve x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7).
explanation: The CRT sum 2·35·2 + 3·21·1 + 2·15·1 = 233 reduces to 23 mod 105, and 23 checks against all three. 233 is the unreduced sum.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
explanation: Reducing exponents mod 6 gives 4 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 14 ≡ 0. 14 is the sum before the final reduction.
concept: Reduce every term, then the sum.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: With superincreasing a' = (171, 197, 459, 1191, 2410) and S = 3798, which bit vector solves the knapsack?
explanation: Greedy from the top takes 2410, 1191 and 197, leaving 0. (1, 0, 0, 1, 1) sums to 3,772, not 3,798.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In Merkle–Hellman with m = 2003, w = 1289 and a'_1 = 2, what is the public weight a_1?
explanation: a_1 = 1289·2 mod 2003 = 2578 − 2003 = 575. 2578 forgets the reduction mod m.
concept: Public weights: a_i = w·a'_i mod m.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why must the Merkle–Hellman modulus m exceed the sum of the secret weights?
option_1: So encryption is faster
option_2: So that w has an inverse and the public key looks random
option_3: So w^−1·S mod m equals the exact superincreasing sum
option_4: So the public key looks random
answer_text: So w^−1·S mod m equals the exact superincreasing sum
explanation: If m > Σa'_i, the reduced value is the true integer sum and the greedy algorithm recovers x. Invertibility of w depends on gcd(w, m) = 1, a separate condition.
concept: m > Σa'_i keeps the decrypted sum exact.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Merkle–Hellman ciphertext S = 6665, w^−1 = 317, m = 2003. What is S' for the greedy step?
explanation: S' = 317·6665 mod 2003 = 2,112,805 mod 2003 = 1643. 2,112,805 is the product before reduction.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Signing and then encrypting gives secrecy and authentication. What is its main cost?
option_1: Four public-key operations per message
option_2: It needs a shared symmetric key
option_3: No authentication of the sender
option_4: The receiver needs the sender's private key
answer_text: Four public-key operations per message
explanation: Sender signs and encrypts, receiver decrypts and verifies, so the slow algorithm runs four times. Each party still uses only its own private key.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which misconception about public-key cryptography is shown by 'AES-256 is stronger than 512-bit RSA'?
option_1: That PKC is inherently more secure than symmetric encryption
option_2: That key management becomes trivial once keys are public
option_3: That PKC replaced symmetric encryption
option_4: That PKC cannot sign messages
answer_text: That PKC is inherently more secure than symmetric encryption
explanation: Strength depends on key length and attack cost, not on whether a cipher is asymmetric. The other two misconceptions concern speed and certificate infrastructure.
concept: Security comes from work factor, not from being public-key.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An eavesdropper sees a Merkle–Hellman public key and ciphertext S but not w or m. What problem must she solve to read the message?
option_1: A superincreasing knapsack
option_2: A general subset-sum instance
option_3: A discrete logarithm modulo m
option_4: Factoring m into primes
answer_text: A general subset-sum instance
explanation: Without the trapdoor the public weights look like an arbitrary knapsack, so she faces general subset sum. Only the receiver, who can undo w, gets the easy superincreasing instance.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Merkle–Hellman rests on an NP-complete problem, yet it was broken. Which explanation is best?
option_1: Its instances are disguised easy knapsacks, not hard average cases
option_2: It used a weak hash function
option_3: NP-complete problems are always easy
option_4: Its keys were too short for the NP-complete hardness to apply
answer_text: Its instances are disguised easy knapsacks, not hard average cases
explanation: NP-completeness is worst-case; the modular disguise of a superincreasing sequence leaves structure that Shamir and lattice reduction exploit. Hardness of the general problem says little about these special instances.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A colleague says public-key cryptography makes certificate authorities unnecessary since keys are public. What is the strongest rebuttal?
option_1: Without authentication an attacker can substitute a fake public key
option_2: CAs are needed because public keys must be kept secret by them
option_3: CAs generate everyone's private keys
option_4: CAs are needed to speed up encryption
answer_text: Without authentication an attacker can substitute a fake public key
explanation: Publishing keys removes the need for secret channels but not the need to bind a key to an identity; a substituted key enables man-in-the-middle. CAs sign that binding, not private keys.
concept: Public keys need authenticity, hence PKI.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: You must compute 7^(10^6) mod 101 by hand in an exam. Which plan is quickest?
option_1: Factor 101 first, then apply the CRT to each prime factor
option_2: Use the CRT with moduli 10 and 10
option_3: Reduce 10^6 mod 100, then square-and-multiply
option_4: Multiply 7 by itself a million times
answer_text: Reduce 10^6 mod 100, then square-and-multiply
explanation: 101 is prime, so the exponent reduces mod 100 to 0, giving 7^0 = 1 immediately. Factoring 101 is pointless as it is prime, and CRT needs coprime moduli whose product is the modulus.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: The security of RSA rests on the difficulty of:
option_1: Factoring n = p·q
option_2: Finding hash collisions
option_3: Computing discrete logarithms
option_4: Solving subset sum
answer_text: Factoring n = p·q
explanation: Anyone who factors n can compute φ(n) and then d. Discrete logarithms underpin Diffie–Hellman and ElGamal instead.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In RSA, how is the private exponent d computed?
option_1: d = e mod φ(n)
option_2: d = e^−1 mod φ(n)
option_3: d = n − e
option_4: d = e^−1 mod n
answer_text: d = e^−1 mod φ(n)
explanation: d must satisfy e·d ≡ 1 mod φ(n) so that M^(ed) ≡ M. Reducing modulo n instead is a classic error.
concept: d is the inverse of e modulo φ(n).
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which condition must the public exponent e satisfy?
option_1: e must be even
option_2: e must be prime to n only
option_3: e must exceed φ(n)
option_4: gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1
answer_text: gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1
explanation: e needs an inverse modulo φ(n), which exists only when they are coprime. An even e always shares the factor 2 with φ(n).
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which items form the RSA public key?
option_2: {d, n}
option_3: {p, q}
option_4: {e, n}
answer_text: {e, n}
explanation: The public key is the exponent e with modulus n. p, q, φ(n) and d must stay secret, since any of them reveals d.
concept: Public: e, n. Secret: d, p, q, φ(n).
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why does square-and-multiply reduce modulo n after every step?
option_1: To hide the exponent bits
option_2: To avoid computing d
option_3: To keep intermediate numbers below n²
option_4: To make the result non-deterministic
answer_text: To keep intermediate numbers below n²
explanation: Reducing each product keeps values bounded, so 2,048-bit exponentiation stays tractable. It does not hide exponent bits; that is why timing attacks work.
concept: Reduce as you go: (a·b) mod n.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In left-to-right square-and-multiply, what happens at a 0 bit of the exponent?
option_1: Only a multiplication
option_2: Only a squaring
option_3: A squaring and a multiplication
option_4: Nothing at all
answer_text: Only a squaring
explanation: Each bit squares the accumulator; a 1 bit also multiplies by the base. This asymmetry is what timing attacks exploit.
concept: Bit 0: square. Bit 1: square then multiply.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why does RSA key generation use probabilistic primality tests instead of trial division?
option_1: Trial division to √n is infeasible for 1,024-bit numbers
option_2: Trial division gives wrong answers for numbers above 512 bits
option_3: Primes cannot be divided
option_4: Probabilistic tests factor the number
answer_text: Trial division to √n is infeasible for 1,024-bit numbers
explanation: Trial division up to √n would need on the order of 2^512 divisions for a 1,024-bit candidate. Primality tests decide primality without finding factors.
concept: Testing primality is far easier than factoring.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which composite number fools the Fermat test for every coprime base?
explanation: 561 = 3·11·17 is the smallest Carmichael number. 35 is caught by base 2, and 97 is prime.
concept: Carmichael numbers defeat the Fermat test.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the maximum error probability of one Miller–Rabin round on a composite n?
explanation: At most a quarter of bases are strong liars, so t rounds err with probability at most (1/4)^t. 1/2 is the Solovay–Strassen bound.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Who first described timing attacks on RSA implementations (1996)?
option_1: Whitfield Diffie
option_2: Paul Kocher
option_3: Adi Shamir
option_4: Daniel Bleichenbacher
answer_text: Paul Kocher
explanation: Kocher showed that decryption time leaks private-key bits. Bleichenbacher is known for the 1998 padding-oracle attack.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How does RSA blinding defeat timing attacks?
option_1: It switches to a smaller modulus
option_2: It shortens the private exponent so every step takes equal time
option_3: It randomises the value being exponentiated
option_4: It encrypts the timing data
answer_text: It randomises the value being exponentiated
explanation: Decrypting C·r^e with a fresh random r makes intermediate values unpredictable to the attacker, and r is divided out afterwards. The key itself is unchanged.
concept: Blinding: work on C·r^e, then remove r.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: If x² ≡ y² (mod n) but x ≢ ±y (mod n), what follows?
option_1: n must be a perfect square, so √n is a factor
option_2: n is a perfect square
option_3: gcd(x − y, n) is a non-trivial factor of n
option_4: x and y are inverses
answer_text: gcd(x − y, n) is a non-trivial factor of n
explanation: n divides (x − y)(x + y) without dividing either factor, so each shares a proper factor with n. This principle drives the quadratic sieve and Miller–Rabin.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: With p = 7, q = 17 and e = 5, what is d?
explanation: φ(n) = 96 and 5·77 = 385 = 4·96 + 1. 96 is φ(n) itself, not the inverse.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: With public key {5, 119}, what is the ciphertext of M = 19?
explanation: 19^5 = 2,476,099 = 20,807·119 + 66. 95 is 19·5, a multiplication instead of exponentiation.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: p = 11, q = 13. Which value is a valid public exponent?
explanation: φ(n) = 120 = 2³·3·5, so e must avoid 2, 3 and 5; only 7 qualifies. 9 shares 3, 15 shares 3 and 5, and 10 shares 2 and 5.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How many squarings does left-to-right square-and-multiply perform for a 12-bit exponent?
explanation: The loop squares once per exponent bit, here 12 times (the first squares 1). 3,532 is the naive multiplication count for 3533.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Computing 9726^3533 mod 11413, the accumulator is 105 after the bit at position 2. Bit 1 is 0. What is the next value?
explanation: A 0 bit means square only: 105² = 11,025, which is below 11,413. 5761 is the final result after the last bit, which is 1.
concept: Follow square, then multiply on 1 bits.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Writing n − 1 = 2^k·m with m odd for n = 561, what are k and m?
explanation: 560 = 16·35, so k = 4 and m = 35 (odd). 70 and 140 are even, so they cannot be m.
concept: Strip all factors of 2 from n − 1.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In Miller–Rabin on 561 with a = 2 the sequence is 263, 166, 67, 1. Why is 561 composite?
option_1: 263 is not equal to 1
option_2: The sequence reached 1, which only composites do
option_3: 561 is odd
option_4: 67 is a square root of 1 other than ±1
answer_text: 67 is a square root of 1 other than ±1
explanation: Modulo a prime, the only square roots of 1 are ±1; 67² ≡ 1 with 67 ≢ ±1 proves compositeness. Reaching 1 through −1 would have been consistent with primality.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Fermat test on n = 35 with base 2 gives 2^34 mod 35 = ?
explanation: 2^32 ≡ 11 and 2^34 ≡ 11·4 = 44 ≡ 9. A prime would give 1, so 35 is composite.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Using 12² ≡ 2² (mod 35), which factor of 35 does gcd(12 − 2, 35) reveal?
explanation: gcd(10, 35) = 5, and gcd(14, 35) = 7 gives the other. 10 is x − y, not the gcd.
concept: gcd(x − y, n) exposes a factor.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In factoring 539873, why are the relations for 735 and 801 combined?
option_1: Their sum equals n
option_2: Their product makes every prime exponent even
option_3: Their squares are both primes
option_4: They are the two smallest values tried above √n
answer_text: Their product makes every prime exponent even
explanation: 2^5·11 times 2^5·11·17² gives 2^10·11²·17², a perfect square, so X² ≡ Y². Including 783 would add an odd power of 13.
concept: Choose relations whose exponent vectors sum to even.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Timing a device computing 5^20 mod 33 reveals slower steps at bit positions 1 and 3 from the left. What exponent pattern is leaked?
explanation: Extra multiplications occur only at 1 bits, so slow steps 1 and 3 spell 1-0-1-0-0 = 20. That is how timing leaks d bit by bit.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why is textbook RSA weak for encrypting 'YES' or 'NO' votes?
option_1: Votes need a hash instead
option_2: RSA cannot encrypt messages shorter than the modulus length
option_3: Deterministic encryption lets anyone encrypt both and compare
option_4: The ciphertext reveals d
answer_text: Deterministic encryption lets anyone encrypt both and compare
explanation: Same plaintext, same ciphertext, so an attacker encrypts each candidate with the public key and matches. Randomised padding such as OAEP removes this.
concept: Textbook RSA is deterministic; pad it.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why must RSA primes be at least 1,024 bits each today?
option_1: Square-and-multiply needs long keys
option_2: Miller–Rabin becomes unreliable for primes below 1,024 bits
option_3: Smaller primes make e impossible
option_4: Number field sieve attacks can factor 512-bit moduli
answer_text: Number field sieve attacks can factor 512-bit moduli
explanation: Sub-exponential factoring has broken 512-bit and 768-bit RSA, so a 2,048-bit modulus is the current floor. The other options are not real constraints.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An RSA user publishes n = 119 and e = 5, and you learn φ(n) = 96. What can you now do?
option_1: Compute d = 77 and decrypt everything
option_2: Only find p, not q
option_3: Nothing; φ(n) is harmless
option_4: Only verify signatures; decryption still needs p and q
answer_text: Compute d = 77 and decrypt everything
explanation: φ(n) gives d directly as e^−1 mod φ(n). It also yields p and q, since p + q = n − φ(n) + 1.
concept: φ(n) is as secret as d.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which RSA operation is typically fastest, and why?
option_1: Decryption, because d is usually smaller than e in practice
option_2: Key generation, because primes are common
option_3: Signing, because hashes are short
option_4: Encryption or verification, because e is small (e.g. 65537)
answer_text: Encryption or verification, because e is small (e.g. 65537)
explanation: A small e with few 1 bits makes M^e cheap, while d is full length. Key generation needs repeated primality testing and is slowest.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A smart-card vendor fixes timing leaks by adding random delays. Which assessment is best?
option_1: Weak: averaging many traces removes noise; use constant time and blinding
option_2: Harmful: delays break RSA correctness
option_3: Sufficient: random delays fully hide all timing differences
option_4: Unnecessary: timing attacks need physical access
answer_text: Weak: averaging many traces removes noise; use constant time and blinding
explanation: Random noise only raises the number of measurements the attacker needs. Constant-time code and blinding remove the data-dependent timing.
concept: Fix side channels at the source.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: For a production RSA key generator, which primality approach is most appropriate?
option_1: Miller–Rabin with many random bases (e.g. 40 rounds)
option_2: Trial division up to √n
option_3: Accepting any odd number ending in 7
option_4: A single Fermat test with base 2 on each odd candidate
answer_text: Miller–Rabin with many random bases (e.g. 40 rounds)
explanation: Forty Miller–Rabin rounds bound the error below 2^−80 cheaply. A Fermat test misses Carmichael numbers and trial division is infeasible.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Design a fast RSA decryption for a busy TLS server holding p and q. What is the best approach?
option_1: Compute C^d mod n with naive multiplication
option_2: Use RSA-CRT with d mod (p−1) and d mod (q−1), plus blinding
option_3: Skip padding to save time
option_4: Choose a tiny private exponent such as d = 3 for speed
answer_text: Use RSA-CRT with d mod (p−1) and d mod (q−1), plus blinding
explanation: CRT gives about 4× speed-up and blinding preserves side-channel resistance. A tiny d is vulnerable to Wiener's attack and skipping padding breaks security.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does the Diffie–Hellman protocol accomplish?
option_1: Hashing passwords
option_2: Encrypting messages directly with the public values
option_3: Producing digital signatures
option_4: Agreeing a shared secret over a public channel
answer_text: Agreeing a shared secret over a public channel
explanation: DH only establishes a key; that key then drives a symmetric cipher. It neither encrypts data nor signs.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is a primitive root modulo a prime q?
option_1: The smallest prime factor of q − 1
option_2: Any number less than q
option_3: An element whose powers produce every value 1 to q − 1
option_4: An element equal to its own inverse modulo q
answer_text: An element whose powers produce every value 1 to q − 1
explanation: A primitive root generates the whole multiplicative group Z_q*. Not every element does: some generate only subgroups.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why do Alice and Bob reach the same DH key?
option_1: Bob sends his secret to Alice
option_2: The key is fixed in advance
option_3: Both compute α raised to X_A·X_B mod q
option_4: They exchange the key encrypted
answer_text: Both compute α raised to X_A·X_B mod q
explanation: (α^X_B)^X_A and (α^X_A)^X_B both equal α^(X_A·X_B) because exponents multiply. The private values never cross the wire.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why can binary search not solve g^x ≡ y (mod p)?
option_1: Exponents must be prime, so the search space has gaps
option_2: Binary search needs floating point
option_3: Modular powers wrap around and are not monotonic
option_4: Modular division is undefined
answer_text: Modular powers wrap around and are not monotonic
explanation: Over the integers 2^x grows steadily, so 'too high/too low' guides the search; modulo p the values jump unpredictably. That loss of ordering is what makes the DLP hard.
concept: No ordering mod p ⇒ no binary search.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)
